speechtext: On the orders of the day:

maintopic: SASKATOON-USE OF ASSEMBLED PARTS SHIPPED FROM MONTREAL
speechtext: I should like to ask the Minister of Reconstruction and Supply what action is being taken in regard to the urgent demand of Saskatoon labour to be allowed to work locally on wartime houses rather than have ready-made assembled parts shipped from Montreal?

speakeroldname: Right Hon. C. D. HOWE (Minister of Reconstruction and Supply):
maintopic: SASKATOON-USE OF ASSEMBLED PARTS SHIPPED FROM MONTREAL
speechtext:
The first wire received from the Saskatoon trades and labour council complained that the material being used was produced by non-union low paid Montreal firms, and the council protested such discrimination and demanded an immediate investigation. The matter was investigated, and I am informed that the company in question does have a labour agreement with its employees, and I have no information that the union, is not active or that the agreement is not in full operation. The trades and labour council were advised that this material was shipped to Saskatoon because of the inability of Wartime Housing to obtain similar material in that area, and that this millwork was being manufactured against standard price lists which were approved by the mill owners association. A high percentage of this millwork is manufactured from white pine, and in normal times the Saskatchewan mills import the lumber from the United States. As such imports are practically non-existent today it is necessary to use eastern pine or the equivalent, and in order to ensure a steady flow of the material to complete housing projects it has been necessary to farm out the required millwork among various eastern firms.
A further wire today protests that the eastern millwork is much inferior to local Saskatoon products and that the building inspectors have expressed disapproval to the Toronto office of Wartime Housing Limited. Further protest is made that the workmanship is inferior, that certain materials have arrived in smashed1 condition, and that the local carpenters union will not install millwork shipped from Montreal received after March 1. The wire also states that the report that the local mills cannot supply on time is false.
We are asking Mr. Russell, vice-president of Wartime Housing, who is now in Vancouver, to return by way of Saskatoon to investigate and attempt to adjust this situation.

speakeroldname: Hon. J. A MacKINNON (Minister of Trade and Commerce):
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, the question has been raised whether or not the employees of the Canadian wheat board should come under the civil service commission. I am informed that this point was considered when the original act was drafted in 1935, and it was felt that the board would be unable to obtain the specialized skill and experience it required if its employees were placed under the Civil Service Act. That is still the feeling of the board and of the government. The wheat board, while a crown corporation, is engaged in a very large commercial undertaking and should be free to choose employees who have the necessary qualifications to carry out the duties required under the act.

The relevant section-of the original act, I take it, is section 5. So far I have not had a chance to check through to see if any change has been made in the wording of that original section. In the amendment now proposed, however, the words "notwithstanding anything contained in the Civil Service Act" are inserted in addition to .the words contained in section 5 of the original act. Were they in any previous amendment?
Those words were not in the previous act.
Are they being put in now just for the purpose of making it more certain that they do not come under the Civil Service Act?
Yes, I would think so; to make it definite.

There is every possibility that this act, though perhaps not considered today as permanent legislation, will become

Canadian Wheat Board Act

such in future; and if it is permanent legislation then I think the staff engaged by the board should be recruited through the civil service commission. If this were a temporary department to carry on for only three or four or five years, a good case could be made out for not having the employees under the Civil Service Act; but when it is likely to become a permanent part of the operations of the government of Canada I can see no reason why this staff should not be engaged in the ordinary way. In his statement a moment ago the minister said this was very important work and that the board should be free to engage its staff any way it could, or words to that effect. I do not see that it is any more important than the Department of Justice, the Department of Finance, or any other department, and in my opinion there is no reason why the staff should not be recruited through the civil service commission.

May I refer to one thing I mentioned yesterday; that is, that recently what is known as the Gordon report was brought down, making certain recommendations that in the near future technical and professional men be taken out from under the Civil Service Act. I can see why technical and professional men might have to be chosen by the board itself, but I can see very little reason why other officers, clerks and employees should not be chosen by the civil service commission.

I am not sure that this point is in the mind of the mover of this amendment, or of any one in the committee, but I think it fair to make the statement that in the seven years during which I have been intimately connected with the board, in not a single case has there been the acceptance of a political recommendation as to personnel. I remember once getting a letter from a stenographer who had lived in Edmonton and who was out of work in Winnipeg. I wrote the Canadian wheat board asking them to have this stenographer interviewed and taken on if possible. They interviewed her, but they did not take her on, and I did not try it again. I am sure no one else has tried, either.
You have no influence at all.

I should like to mention one other feature. It may be possible that the wheat board will become a permanent institution. In that event how about the staff of the wheat board enjoying superannuation privileges, as they would under the Civil Service Act? It seems hardly fair that they should not have that privilege.
[Mr. MacInnis.J

The matter of superannuation benefits for the staff has been considered, and I think something will have to be done about it. It is something that cannot be decided quickly; there are important considerations to be worked out, but the matter has been before the wheat committee of the cabinet, and it is a matter of concern to the wheat board.

I was interested in the statement of the minister that there had been no political influence in connection with appointments under this organic zation. As yet no one has suggested that there was any political influence; but on the other hand we have not heard any reason why the ordinary staff of this organization should not be treated in the same way as other members of the civil service. I quite agree as to the expert end of the picture. I agree with the hon. member for Vancouver East. Either the civil service commission is worth while or it is not. If it is worth while it should have jurisdiction over this organization, just as it has over any other department of government; and I have yet to hear any reason from the minister as to why that statement is not correct.

Employment under the Canadian wheat board varies a great deal through the crop year. There are large seasonal increases in staff, and that is one reason why I do not think it advisable to bring them under the civil service commission, particularly at this time.

This question has been before the committee quite frequently. The statement made by the minister is not satisfactory. For example, the Department of Agriculture has a large number of personnel who are taken on a temporary basis during the crop season. If the salaries that prevail in the civil serive at the present time are not high enough to attract the type of person necessary to administer an organization such as the wheat board, then the whole scale of salaries in the civil service should be revised. It is important that the employees of the wheat board should be placed in exactly the same position as employees of all other departments of government. If necessaiy the minister should recommend an upward revision of salaries.

This is an important principle. If I may make a comparison with another board, I have had many complaints from field inspectors of the old soldier settlement board. They have become almost a permanent board in the country. I have

Because of age and for other reasons many of them have had to leave their jobs, and they do not get the retirement benefits enjoyed by other civil servants. They do not get proper recognition. I can visualize this board becoming more or less permanent; the employees should be given the same recognition as other civil servants. speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
Perhaps I should give an answer to one part of that question. I do not know anything about the advice received from the Canadian advisory committee; but the hon. member for Lake Centre did ask some questions about the constitutional bases of this legislation which perhaps should be answered at an early stage in the discussion.
The opinion of the law officers of the crown is that the bill as drafted is within the constitutional powers of the dominion parliament. Naturally that is so; otherwise the government would not have introduced it.
The bill is the exercise of the poiver of the dominion parliament to regulate interprovincial and export trade and commerce in wheat produced in designated areas. It is contemplated that interprovincial and export trade and commerce in wheat from that area shall be directed through one channel, namely, the Canadian wheat board. There may be other constitutional bases upon which the legislation can be set, but the main reliance for the
Canadian Wheat Board Act

constitutionality of the legislation is upon the trade and commerce power in section 91 of the British North America Act. It may also be authorized under power to legislate for the peace, order and good government of Canada, and so forth, but it will not be necessary for me to go into these other powers. We believe the power to regulate interprovincial and export trade and commerce is amply sufficient to enable this parliament to pass this legislation.
It should be understood that the producer will have the option of selling the wheat which he grows either into interprovincial or export markets through the Canadian wheat board, or, alternatively, into local markets in the provinces, which he may do himself, not through the Canadian wheat board.
The quota control is based upon our jurisdiction over elevators and mills designated as for the general advantage of Canada, and over railways. There may be other constitutional bases for that quota control, but certainly the fact that these mills and elevators have been designated as for the general advantage of Canada and that we have jurisdiction over railways, gives us jurisdiction over the quota control provided for by the act. These are the general observations that apply to the constitutional bases for the legislation.
The hon. member for Lake Centre yesterday seemed to be under the impression that the passage of this legislation was sought in the exercise of emergency powers, and he made some reference to certain decisions of the privy council in connection with emergency powers. But those are not the constitutional grounds for the legislation. What were the other questions?
The other questions referred to reports from the advisory committee to the board or to the government. Shall I read it? It is reported at page 817.

The hon. member for Lake Centre asked whether a report had been received from the advisory committee in regard to the question of bilateral agreements. No. There was no report. A further question was whether the wheat board was asked its opinion in regard to the agreement with Britain. I thought the way in which the hon. member for Lake Centre asked the question yesterday was whether the advisory committee was asked its opinion in regard to the agreement with Britain, but I see in Hansard now that the question is whether the wheat board was asked its opinion in regard to that agreement. I am not sure at the moment whether the wheat board was asked its opinion, but I do remem-

ber the board giving us a lengthy confidential opinion on this point. Such an opinion passing between the wheat board and myself would be, I think, a privileged document.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Is the hon. gentleman asking about a report from the advisory committee or from the wheat board?
I am asking about the report or recommendation from the wheat board which the minister himself mentioned.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I have been a member of an informal committee of the cabinet which has existed for many years, called the wTheat committee or the wheat subcommittee of the cabinet. That committee meets frequently with the Canadian wheat board and discusses with the wheat board matters sometimes of policy and sometimes of administration. But certainly the understanding throughout the years has always been that those discussions with the wheat board are of the same nature as discussions with groups of departmental officials, and certainly it would be introducing an innovation to make public the recommendations that we get from the Canadian wheat board. I am afraid that the reports would lose some of their value to the government if it were expected that they were for the public, and the position we have always taken with regard to reports of that kind is that they are privileged and confidential communications.

Perhaps fools rush in where angels fear to tread, but it appears to me that after all the wheat board is or should be the servant of the people and of the house, and if the boprd made a recommendation with respect to the wheat agreement, prior to its execution by the government, the committee is entitled to know it. The minister may have
stated his view, but I do not think we on this side can accept that view. I have made my
statement.

As Minister of Agriculture, and as a member from the west when this committee was set up, I think I ought to say a word or two with regard to the remarks *which have just been made. The old board, as it was prior to the coming into power of the government under the present Prime Minister, was one which was set up under the act, with certain advisers on it. It was a type of board with which some people were not entirely satisfied; and when the government came into power in 1935 and selected a new board of three, the chairman of that board refused to act if there was to be any advisory committee. He took the position conditional upon there being no advisory committee until he had completed the task which was assigned to him. Mr. Murray was then chairman of the board. When Mr. Murray had completed the task that was assigned to him, which was that of getting rid of the great surplus of wheat which had piled up under the board as it had been operated previously, he resigned from the board; then a new board was set up. An advisory committee was appointed at the request of the organized farmers of western Canada to begin with, and they insisted that there should be on that committee a majority representation of the farmers. The committee was set up with its present number, and for the first time including representatives from eastern Canada. Prior to that the advisory committee was composed of western men. I think I am right when I say this, although I am speaking entirely from memory: I do not think those men are paid any salary. They are men who are engaged in their own lines of business. Mr. Wesson is president of the Saskatchewan pool. Mr. Campbell is a miller; Mr. Smith is a grain dealer in the city of Winnipeg, but at one time was a member of the board and so on; one could go through the names of the group. These men come together from time to time, and they advise. I do not understand that they advise the government; I may be wrong about that. I understand that they advise the wheat board.

I do not know whether the act requires them to make a report to the government.
No; it advises the board.

I did not think the act required them to make a report to the government. I am not sure that I am right in saying that they make a report to the board as such. They meet along with the board and discuss questions with respect to the marketing of wheat. They enter upon and discuss these matters very much in the same way as members of the government do. Their point of view is put down in the minutes of the meeting. By the time they are through discussing it they may all have changed their minds. They talk about what should be done with regard to this or that; and it is not a report in the ordinary sense of the term. What these men say individually with regard to the matter may have more to do with what the concern they represent really thinks about it; but they give the knowledge and information they have to the board, to be considered by the board when they are arriving at decisions with regard to the marketing of wheat.
I think that explanation in itself would indicate that the discussions are not the kind of thing that can be placed before the public. These men are there giving their point of view. They may have strong objections to that point of view being spread all over Canada, particularly if it is a point of view that was later reconsidered and a different decision arrived at. I think these men would be quite justified in saying that if everything they said in those meetings, for the consideration of the board, everything put down in the form of minutes, was to be given to the public, they -would not act in an advisory capacity; or if they did act, they would not express their views freely in the interests of the board itself or in the interests of the people of western Canada who are marketing wheat. I think it would be improper to have minutes of that kind published at all, either before the house or otherwise. I would point out that it is not the kind of committee some members seem to think it is. It is not a committee to advise the government. It is not a committee to advise anyone other than the wheat board.

How many times has this advisory committee met during the past year? Does the wheat board always accept its advice? If not, how many times during the past year did the wheat board not act on its advice?

So did every other member of the wheat committee; so did every member of the wheat board. But after we had discussed the whole matter and arrived at a conclusion as to what we were going to do, we might not all have agreed . on every detail of the policy entered into, but looking at the policy as a whole we did agree with it and finally announced it to the country and brought it before this house.
That is what the country is interested in. The people are not interested in any small differences of opinion there might have been

between either members of the government or members of the board. Nor are they interested in the small differences of opinion that existed between the members of the advisory committee. What they are interested in is that a group of some twenty men, working together over a period) of time, finally arrived at a conclusion and submitted that conclusion to this house. So far as I can find out from listening to the discussion, that conclusion has almost one hundred per cent support in this house; so why should we not get on with the legislation?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
Well, Mr. Chairman, I have given the point some consideration, though perhaps not enough; perhaps more consideration is necessary, but the conclusion I have reached1 is that the clause declaring the board to be an agent of the crown should remain in the act; first, because it appears to be a statement of reality, of the substantial facts of the case. One very important part of this measure is being enacted to enable a contract with Great Britain to be carried out, a con-

Canadian Wheat Board Act
tract which was made between the government of Canada and the government of Great Britain. In essence and in substance the board which carries out that contract, through which all the wheat from a designated area going into interprovincial and export markets must be channeled, is acting for the government which made the contract. So I think it is wise to recognize the facts and realities of the situation and say they are the agents of the crown. In the second place the act contains provisions making the board subject to the directions of the governor in council, and I think it would be anomalous to set up a board subject to the directions of the governor in council, carrying out regulations passed by the governor in council, and carrying out the policy of the government, unless it were regarded as an agency of the government. In the only ease that has come before the courts where the matter was in issue it has been held, even without this statement, that the board is an agent of the crown in fact, and I think it is pretty hard to get away from that. I cannot see any advantage in saying it is not an agent of the crown, and I believe that is what we would have to do if we were to go on the other theory.
I think what I said last evening, without too much consideration, in regard to certain advantages was not very strong. I do not believe it had too much substance in it. That is. while it is true that as agent for the crown the board does not need to pay local taxes or provincial taxes, I do not believe that is a very important point. Possibly the board would want to pay municipal taxes on real estate occupied by its offices. I do not know about that, but it wrnuld be a very small factor in the situation. On the wheat owned by the board I doubt whether there ever would be any municipal or provincial taxation. So while my statement with regard to taxation was true, in my judgment that is not an important matter. There might be provincial statutes, such as licensing statutes, which would embarrass the board in its operations if it were not set up as an agency of the crown. That consideration might become important, but I doubt it. The other consideration I mentioned, that the farmers would not be exempt from garnishee proceedings if the board were not set up as an agency of the crown is somewhat doubtful, in the light of other provisions in the act which were brought to my attention after I made the statement last evening. Under those provisions the participation certificates are not assignable, and if they are not assignable perhaps participation payments are not subject to garnishment proceedings anyway, so I do not think those arguments are very strong.
Personally I believe proceedings should be in the Exchequer Court of Canada rather than in magistrate's courts or district courts or county courts or trial divisions of superior courts in the various provinces, and I believe that result is obtained by having the board set up as an agency of the crown. One reason the Exchequer Court of Canada is the appropriate tribunal for the settlement of suits against the Canadian wheat board is that if actions were brought in perhaps several or many of these other courts such as magistrate's courts, county courts, district courts and the other courts I have mentioned with respect to small matters-and the board has had a bit of experience in that regard already-the natural reaction would be that the board would have to hold up distribution until the matter went through the various courts and was settled. It might delay considerably the distribution of the money. I realize that the same might be true if it were in the Exchequer Court of Canada, but at any rate you do not have the danger of the diversity of judgments in inferior courts that you would have if actions could be brought in the various courts. Therefore for these reasons I think that that section should remain. That is the best consideration I have been able to give it so far. It may be that there are other considerations which should be taken into account.

Section 1, subsection 1, as it is in the original act, reads:
The board shall be a body corporate having capacity to contract and to sue and be sued in the name of the board.
Subsection 2 of section 2 which the minister is submitting to the committee for approval reads:
The board is, for all purposes, an agent of His Majesty in right of Canada, and its powers under this act may be exercised by it only as an agent of His Majesty in the said right.
That is like giving the answer yes and no to the same question. Is the board responsible in contract? Is it responsible in tort? You cannot overlook the effect of the Interpretation Act of the dominion which says:
No provision or enactment in any act shall affect, in any manner whatsoever, the rights of His Majesty, his heirs or successors, unless it is expressly stated therein that His Majesty shall be bound thereby.
This bill in clause 2 says in effect that His Majesty will not be bound by it, by saying that the board is in effect a servant of His Majesty. Yet in the prior section it says that they can sue and be sued. I believe it has
Canadian Wheat Board Act

been decided in the highest court of Ontario that the words "sue and be sued" apply only to contracts. It does not apply to any action in tort. It does not apply perhaps to a crime. I would say that this subsection should be widened to cover every kind of liability, and if subsection 2 is made for the purpose which the minister has stated, it should have the words tacked on to the front of it that it is subject to the provisions of subsection 1.
So far as magistrates courts are concerned, if there are such courts in the provinces they would deal only with small matters or with criminal matters. So far as any other small courts are concerned they can deal only with matters of small moment and their judgment would not be binding on any other court. There will be judgments of the highest courts which will be binding on the lower courts. I would submit that where the board is going to spend millions of dollars there should be some redress on the part of those who deal with it. They should not have to get a fiat; they should not have to come to Ottawa and have the case tried before the exchequer court. I do not think the exchequer court was ever intended to decide cases such as this. The exchequer court was first brought into existence for a very different purpose, and long before these crown companies were so numerous and so important as they are now. I respectfully submit that the minister should take into consideration the widening of subsection 1 and the insertion before subsection 2 of the words:
That, subject to the provisions of subsection 1 of this section . . .
Only in this tvay can they do justice to the people who are to deal with the wheat board.
Mr.-ILSLEY: The hon. gentleman does not say that they could be sued only on contracts, does he?

I think the definition of "producer" is wide enough to cover all grain. I cannot see how the grain can come from any other body than the producers. If this amount is so small, I would suggest that it be paid to the producers anyway, and that we delete this section. Otherwise the board would be left a good deal of leeway with regard to the disposal of the producers' grain.
There may be losses.

I wish to support the hon. member for Melfort in his contention. I also think this is an unnecessary clause. I am informed that every year the board requires to buy small quantities of wheat that has gone out of the hands of the producer entirely and possibly outside the designated area; it is to cover those cases that this authority is being asked for.

What has been done with the profits on those transactions in the past? Have they been given back to the producers, or have they been put in the general revenue fund? The minister just now said there have been no profits paid into the general revenue fund in the past. Where did they go? Did they go to the producer? If they went to the producer in the past, why should they not go to the producer in the future?
Has there in past years been any grain marketed, say by the sheriff or the bailiff, where the producer did not get the benefit of participation?
I do not think so.
What amount of grain has been bought by the board during the last year other than from producers? I think we should have that information before we pass this section.
I think I can have that information for the hon. member tomorrow.
From the discussion I gather that the amounts involved here, which the government is planning to put into the consolidated revenue fund, are not very large?
That is right.

I respectfully urge that the suggestions put forward ought to be sympathetically considered. The expenses of this board are being charged back against the farmer. Why, then, should not any of these little benefits arising from the operations of the board go to his credit and be divided up with the other balances that are paid out in participation certificates?

I would ask the minister to give serious consideration to deleting subsection 2 of the section under consideration. It refers to only small quantities of grain. I do not see why it should be retained. I would ask the minister to delete the part concerned
with the paying of the amounts into the consolidated revenue fund. If the section is necessary to give the board power to buy those small amounts of grain that may appear here and there-and I cannot see how they can appear unless there is a black market of some kind in operation in regard to the pool-then it is all right. But I do not see why any profit made with respect to this operation should not be paid out to the producers as a whole, because the producers as a whole are paying the expenses as a whole.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: As I understand the situation, the profits talked of here are not profits on the grain of the producers who have participation certificates. There may be some profits, or there may be losses from the handling of other grain; and the question is whether those profits are to go in with and those losses taken out of the money before it is distributed among the producers of other grain or whether the transactions are to be for the account of the consolidated revenue fund, the government taking the small profit or loss as the case may be. I do not think it is a matter of great consequence to the government, but it would appear to me that the fairness of the case is as expressed in the statute, that what the farmer is entitled to is a division of the profits on his grain; and that to charge up against him losses if they are losses, and credit him with profits, if there are profits, on somebody else's grain, is mixing two things.
I do not think the board has power to buy grain grown outside the designated area.
It has taken that power. The suggestion is made that that power be given to the board.

Well, the minister should give some consideration to the matter. I should like to see the amounts involved in this during the last year, and where they came from, so that we can deal intelligently with it. I do not think we can, without knowing what is involved.

In reading over this section, I should like to ask the minister to explain what is meant by:
Profits, if any, realized by the board from its operations under this act during any crop year, other than from its operations under part III, with respect to the disposition of which no provision is made elsewhere in this act.
And then:
Losses, if any, sustained by the board (a) from its operations under part III.
One part contains the expression "other than from its operations under part III", and the
Canadian Wheat Board Act

other contains the expression "losses, if any, sustained by the board from its operations under part III".

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I believe I can explain that. Losses, under the second part of the section, whether they are under the producers' account or not, are charged to the consolidated revenue fund. In the earlier part of the section, profits, if made not on the producers' account, go into the consolidated' revenue fund. The change that has been suggested is that the profits on certain grain be distributed among the producers of other grain. Certainly, if that change were to be made, in fairness the second part of the last section should come out, too, and the losses should be charged to those producers-if there are losses. But in any event the government would have to bear the losses from its operations under part III, and they would have to be careful there were not losses, through fixing their prices at proper levels, and so on. But if there are losses the government would have to bear them.
Do I understand that the government is guaranteeing to the farmer $1.35 regardless of what is left in the fund at the end' of 1950?
Yes.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Indubitably.

The explanation given a moment ago by the Minister of Justice may be all right, if it applies only to the small amounts of grain which may be picked up here and there. Then possibly it might be allowed to come in. But what is in the minds of most producers is that the board may be operating in coarse grains. That is not what the board is set up to do .under section 3. In dealing in those coarse grains it could have the profits from the operation on coarse grains going into the consolidated revenue fund, or the losses charged to that fund. I think that is really where the sticker comes in.
We feel that if the board is going to handle coarse grains-and we contend that it should^-a separate pool should be set up so that the profits and losses in connection therewith can be handled in that way. If there is only a small amount of grain involved, then I believe, if an answer is given to the hon. member for Melfort as to how much, and where from, we can get over the section easily.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
I understand the hon.
member to say that the only exception to the rule that profits go into the consolidated revenue fund, in the provision as drawn, is profits from the operations under part III

which is confined to wheat alone. He says, if a pool were set up for the handling of coarse grains, and a profit were made, even though the regulations setting up that pool contemplated the division of the profit among the farmers-and the losses, if there were any, taken from the consolidated revenue fund- that, even so, those regulations could be overruled or overridden by the express provision of the section, that the profits could not be paid back to the farmer in dealing with coarse grains, and that the government is depriving itself of the power to set up a pool along the same lines as the wheat pool. Is that the hon. member's position?

Yes; that is the way it
looks to many of us.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
I doubt whether operations
of that kind were contemplated for coarse grains. However I think there is enough in the fears expressed by the hon. member to warrant further consideration. It was never intended to arrive at that result. That was not the intention of the section at all. It was assumed that if there were pools in coarse grains in the future they should be operated in the same way as the wheat pool, so far as the division of profits, so-called, are concerned.
That is something in the future; there has not been that kind of pool in the past, nor have there been participation certificates, in the ordinary sense, in dealing in coarse grains.-
The hon. member is visualizing a situation which does not exist at all, and is expressing a fear that possibly the section prevents our doing something which he thinks might possibly be desirable in the future.

That is why I said earlier that I thought we should know the government's policy as regards coarse grains. We do not know what its policy will be with regard to coarse grains, and that is why we are not prepared to let this section pass in its present form. Either provision should be made for the pooling of coarse grains, if that is to be the government's intention under the bill or some other provision should be made. That is why we thought we should be told the government's policy with respect to coarse grains, so that we might know exactly what this section means.

I should like to ask a
hypothetical question. The Minister of Trade and Commerce said that the board would likely be providing an alternative marketing method for coarse grains. Supposing for the 1947 crop the board bought from the farmers

Canadian Wheat Board Act
10,000,000 bushels of barley and made ten cents a bushel on it, or SI million; what would be the general method of distributing that money?

We have had no assurance from the government until today, as I understand it, that there would be further payment on coarse grains for last year, if a profit were made. We do not know what the government's policy with regard to coarse grains is to be in 1947. If it is to be what it is today, with the ceiling and floor prices remaining as they are, and if the government sells large quantities of coarse grain into the export market at the export price, and farmers receive only the payments on certificates that they are receiving today, namely, ten cents on oats and fifteen cents on barley, large sums of money will be accruing to the government as a result of these sales of coarse grains. We want to know whether the farmers are to get it or whether it is to be paid into consolidated revenue fund. Under this provision it could be paid into the fund.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: If a pool were operated on the same basis as the pool in wheat, that would never do. That was never contemplated.
It is possible under the section as it stands.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I think we shall have to look at that part of the section to see whether it does prevent a pool being set up. It might be desirable in the future some time, but it has not happened in the past.

I do not think it is the intention of the government to take the profits made out of coarse grains and put them into the consolidated revenue fund. It would be foolish of the government to consider doing that. I think we should know definitely what this section covers before we pass it, and I would suggest that it stand.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Might we have that part of it stand?

Further down on the page is a subsection dealing with investments and I should like to make a few remarks on that. We realize that if the government are determined to have the long-term pool they are setting up here they will need to have some means of investing the money they will have on hand. At the same time I think the government should know' that this is one part of the bill about which the majority of the farmers of western Canada are somewhat hesitant. This board will have in its possession for a considerable length of time large amounts of money wdiich really belong to the farmer. There was a long period prior to the so-called
wartime prosperity; we are entering a period about which many of us are not too optimistic and there would be a considerable amount of money tied up in this fund.
I realize that I may be on the borderline of discussing detail and principle, but I cannot let this section pass without suggesting to the minister that he and his colleagues should give serious consideration to adopting another principle, that the farmer should be entitled to parity prices for his products, and have the participation certificates bring those prices up in one way or another. The government is going to operate a five-year pool and the greater part of that time is before us. Funds will accumulate, and I just want to warn the government that it is going to be difficult to sell the farmers on this idea.

I W'ould support w'hat the hon. member for Humboldt has said. During the next year or tw'o there will be millions of dollars available for investment. No doubt that money will be invested in dominion government securities, but does the board intend to invest that money in securities which are guaranteed against loss, or will it be invested in securities on which losses may be sustained? There is a government security being issued now which is 100 per cent guaranteed.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: That w'ould not be eligible for this type of investment. Canada savings bonds are limited to individuals, with a maximum investment of S2,000.

The producers should bs guaranteed against loss on the investment of their funds. Government bonds are above par and they may stay above par, but in case of serious world conditions and deflation it is quite possible that those bonds would drop considerably below par. This money belong? to the growers; the government is just holding it in trust and there should be no risk involved.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: This is a trust fund and the trustees could buy certain securities. While there is some chance of profit and some chance of loss, he is protected if there is a loss and of course he accounts for the profit. To do it another way would mean the creating of a new type of security with no chance of appreciation and no chance of depreciation.
And with a nominal rate of interest.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
That would require some special legislation, although there may be some power to do it under order in council. I do not know whether this proposal would meet with the approval of the members of the house, or whether it would be agreeable to

the government. I do not think anyone has thought of creating a new type of security for these moneys and fixing an appropriate rate of interest. Is that what the hon. member is suggesting?

That is what I am suggesting. Large sums of money are involved and, since this is really a deferred payment, the growers should not have to take any risk. I think the government would be well advised to give consideration to the proposal the minister has outlined. I think that would be more satisfactory to the producers than the present arrangement. The present arrangement may be all right, but I think the producers would be better satisfied with the minister's suggestion.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
An appropriate rate of
interest for a short-term loan to the government would be pretty low if it were based on ordinary principles.

I do not think the producers would be worried so much about the rate of interest; they are more worried about the security. I can assure the government that, if the bonds in which this money was invested should go down, they will leave themselves open to a tremendous amount of criticism from the producers. For their own protection I think they would be well advised to do as the minister has suggested.

Further in that connection, no doubt the board must have considerable advances, in one way or another, in handling the year's business, and I should like to know what rate of interest the board has paid for the use of the money so advanced during past years. If you have a considerable sum of money tied up in securities for a considerable time, in the first place you may cause the producers to pay interest on money borrowed for the current year's operations; then at the end of the period of time, when your pool is being settled up, you may find it necessary to dispose of the securities in which you have invested your money at a loss. Then the producer is paying from both ends. As a result, it is all the more necessary, as mentioned by the Minister of Justice and the hon. member for Melfort, that the producers should at least have an assurance that there will be no loss on the securities. Otherwise it will be very difficult to put this over with the farmers.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Is any question being asked?
How much does the board require in the line of credit during the course of a year to finance its operations, and what interest does it pay on that money?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: The amounts vary with the size of the crop, the rate at which the producers deliver the crop, and the rate at which it is sold. The interest paid is three per cent.

To get over the difficulty of finding a safe investment for this money, why should the government not pay that money to those entitled to it at the end of two or three years? I am not suggesting that the government should pay out the surplus every year, but I do not understand why they should not pay out the money at the end of two or three years, let us say. As the Minister of Agriculture pointed out the other daj% we are about three years behind now. Why should not payment be made at the end of three years instead of waiting for the five-year period? In that way you -would overcome some of your difficulty in finding a safe investment for this money.

Of course that would
involve a change in the government's policy with regard to the payment of participation certificates. Whether or not they are prepared to do that, I do not know.
That is what I am asking.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Is it suggested that we pay out some of this money before we know how we are coming out on the pool?
Before the end of the five-year period.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Who knows whether we will break even until we are near the end of the five-year period, at any rate?

On the other hand, the farmers know very well that today they are suffering a loss of fifty or seventy-five cents a bushel under the agreement with Great Britain. Surely the government should be prepared to take some risk of a loss, in view of the fact that they are asking the farmers to stand that loss today.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
I do not know whether I should get into this controversy too deeply, because no doubt this matter has been debated a great deal. The principles of this contract are, I think, these; for the protection of floors throughout the later years of the contract, the part of the contract beyond the period we can foresee; for the protection of the United Kingdom government's agreement to have regard to the fact that in the early years of the contract less than world market prices were paid; in return for the protection of those two factors the farmer is accepting less in the earlier year or years of

Canadian Wheat Board Act
the contract than the world market price. Arguments can be advanced both ways as to whether that is a paying bargain for the government to make on behalf of the farmers, but at least the farmers get the advantage of a considerable degree of stability, and I believe a good many consider it less speculative from the viewpoint of the farmer than if he were to take all he could get at the moment with the chance of getting very little during the latter part of the contract.
Then it has been very fairly said by the hon. member for Melfort, who spoke the other night, that he does not think this plan should be set up on a basis of loss to the government or, I should think, of any substantial risk of loss to the government. The view has been expressed that a policy which is put on the basis of the taxpayers' contribution to the wheat grower is not a good policy. The government therefore must make a payment low enough to obviate the danger of any substantia! risk of loss, and therefore it should not make a payment out of this pool too early in the course of the pool and run the risk of loss later on. I do not know the answer to that. The hon. member for Acadia says the farmer is taking less for his wheat nowT than he could get if there were no contract and that therefore the government should take some risk of loss. But the farmer is taking less than he could get for his wheat at the present time because he is assured of a certainty in the latter part of the period. I do not believe that imposes any obligation upon the taxpayers of Canada, through the government, to take any substantial risk of loss by a premature payment out of the pool.

I am merely suggesting that probably at the end of three years the board will have accumulated a fairly large sum of money. We have a guarantee that a certain amount will be received in the last two years. By the end of three years we should have some idea as to the position, and it should be possible then to make a payment. I am not suggesting that the total amount of money on hand should be paid out, but by the end of three years you should be in a safe position to make a payment.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
Well, w'e shall see about that. Perhaps that might be the case, and there might have to be new legislation or something of the kind which would be justified under those conditions. But of course a great many factors would have to be taken into account. For instance, if you had an enormous crop the last year at frightfully low
prices, that would upset your calculations tremendously, as the hon. gentleman can understand.

Perhaps the minister would go a step farther. He said that we might have a tremendous crop in the last year, and in that case no doubt the elevators would be plugged. Would the Minister of Trade and Commerce still propose to accept for delivery, in that case, the grain that could not be taken by the elevators by July 31, 1950?
According to the statement I made, we propose to take all the wheat for which we can find space. We will take all the wheat produced to the extent of the available elevator capacity.
What is to be the determining factor?
We come to that later. It comes under another section.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
As I understand it, we are on section 3 of the bill, and I understood that section 5 of the act, subsections 2 and 3 stood. Is that right?
We are now on 5A (1)?
Yes.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Is that carried?

I wish to ask a
question before it carries. Subsection 5 of this section, which is found on page 5 of the bill, reads:
The board shall make all purchases and sales of securities authorized by this section through the agency of the Bank of Canada.
There will be no commissions paid on these securities? They will not be purchased through a broker or agent?
No.

I should like to refer to
subsection 5 of section 3 which refers to the accounts of the board. The hon. member for Souris read from the records of the agriculture committee dealing with the reports of the board which had been tabled and placed before that committee. When the minister was replying he also read from the findings of the agriculture committee on the reports of the board which had been submitted to it. One of the clauses which he read stated that the agriculture committee had commended the government for having had the annual statements placed each year before the agriculture committee. Immediately we commended the government for that action, they stopped submitting reports of the board to the committee.

Not for that reason.

Probably not for that
reason, but we have not had one since. I do not think they should use the reason which was suggested, namely, that we were so busy that the agriculture committee could not be set up by the government, if the government had seen fit to do so. The reports of the board could have been dealt with each year. I wish to say as strongly as I can that I think that should be done. We should not allow the board's reports to get behind two or three years. Such an action does not give the committee a fair chance to deal with them in a manner in which they could be dealt with. I may say that it does not need to come under this section but in a later section of the bill which provides for reports of the board being tabled. In that particular section, provision should be made which will make it mandatory on the government to submit the board's reports to some committee of the house, either the agriculture committee, the public accounts committee or some special committee, and it should be done annually.
Have we disposed of section 5B under section 3?
Yes.

That is what I understood
the hon. member for Melfort was dealing with.
Yes, it is in that section.

I am in accord with that,
and I believe other hon. members of this group agree with me. We believe that something should be written into section 5B perhaps paragraph (b), to make it compulsory that these reports, when laid upon the table of the house, be referred to the agriculture and colonization committee or some other committee. The suggestion made by the hon. member for Melfort was a good one, and 1 concur in it.

I had not noticed that it came under this section; I thought it came under a later section. Section 5B (2) is the section which deals with this. It reads:
The minister shall lay a copy of each report of the board made under paragraph (e) of subsection 1 of this section before parliament within fifteen days after the receipt thereof by him if parliament is then sitting . . .
There should be an amendment to this subsection stating that the report should be submitted annually to some committee of the house, I would suggest to the agriculture committee.
Order. The hon. member suggested that what he had in mind might come under some other section, and we carried this section.
It was my mistake. I did not realize that it actually came under this section.
Section 5 (2) under section 3 of the bill is carried. We are now dealing with section 5 (3).
Section 5B (2) on page 5 of the bill is the one which I should like to see amended, so that the report would go annually before a committee of the house.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I think I am correct in saying that there is no such provision in any legislation relating to the Canadian National Railways, and yet every year a committee is set up and the report of the railway is referred to that committee. The House of Commons does that itself each year. We are quite willing as a government to give assurance that we shall facilitate similar procedure here and refer it each year; but we do not wish to introduce into the House of Commons legislation by which this parliament tells another parliament or another House of Commons what to do. The report will be on the table and they can do exactly wThat they wish about the report. They have as much right to deal with that report as we have. So long as we say as a government that, so far as we are concerned, we shall move that the report be referred to the agriculture committee, which we are quite prepared to do each year, to facilitate its consideration in every way possible, and put in here that it must be laid on the table, that should be sufficient. I think we have to trust future Houses of Commons to refer it to the committee, if they wish to do so.
I have not the exact reference here, but I am certain that I asked in 1&45 that the report be placed before the agriculture committee. The present government were in power and they did not do so.
If the minister gives the assurance he suggests we of this group would be content with that assurance.

The assurance the hon. member asks for is that the report of the Canadian wheat board be tabled annually as early as possible and that it be referred to the agriculture and colonization committee. We give that assurance.

Canadian Wheat Board Act
The minister will have that done if the government happens to be in power.
That is right.
There is one point that the Minister of Justice can clear up for me. Is it a fact that any member of a standing committee of the house can ask that it be called?
Any hon. member can move to have it called.
That does not necessarily mean that it wall be called.
It is in the hands of the house.

I agree with the position taken by the Minister of Justice and the Minister of Trade and Commerce, but I am surprised at the lack of faith of the hon. gentlemen to my right when they ask that this government give assurance that they will see that the report does come before parliament when it is laid on the table. Suppose this government is not in office-and I presume that is what hon. members to my right hope- what is the value of the assurance which the ministers give?
Section 3 stands.
On section 4-Governor in council to direct the board.

Subsection 4 of this bill repeals sections 7 and 8 of the old act and implements a new section 7 under which the governor in council is given certain powers to direct the board as to the manner in which any of its operations, powers and duties under this act shall be conducted, exercised or performed. I suppose a certain amount of power is handed to the governor in council in most of these eases, but subsection 2 states:
Except as directed by the governor in council, the board shall not buy grain, other than wheat.
It seems to me that this subsection defeats to a large extent the purpose of the bill. If the purpose of the bill is to arrange for orderly marketing, or compulsory marketing, of you wish to use that term, but I say organized marketing-
It does not say that.
I think it is generally understood that the purpose of this bill is to establish orderly marketing.
I cannot agree with the hon. member.

The hon. member may have his own opinion.
This section leaves the handling of coarse grains, rye and flax seed by the board entirely as a matter of discretion with the governor in council. We are opposed to the excepting of these grains from the operation of the act and we object to the way in which it is done here. We think parliament should decide whether or not the board should handle coarse grains and grains other than wheat. If the principle of orderly marketing is accepted, and we are putting a bill through to arrange for that; if it is accepted as a principle in the handling of wheat, why should it not be equally valuable in the handling of coarse grains and rye and flax? If it is good for one it should apply to the other.
So far as our long-term agreements and contracts with other countries are concerned, if we are to have the policy of long-term agreements, under which alone we can have security for the farmer, then the organized marketing of grain will become essential ; and if we are to have long-term agreements with regard to deliveries of meat, bacon, hogs, cattle and beef, then for the same reason we shall have to have orderly marketing of coarse grains. The two things are closely linked together and, if the grain exchange system of handling grains lies in the balance, subject to the whims of order in council, the whims of the government, it is not a healthy condition either for the government or for the board of grain commissioners or for the wheat board.
If we are to make a job of trying out this method that is proposed, why not make a good job of it? If it is a measure we are to try for a few years, it is only right that powers for the handling of other grains should be included in the act.
I am sure that would have the support of hon. members to my right, because if they will look at section 14 of the original act they wili find that it reads:
The governor in council may approve of the provisions of this act being made applicable to oats, barley, rye or flax produced in the provinces of Manitoba. Saskatchewan, Alberta and British Columbia, if the board recommends that such approval be given, whereupon the provisions of this act shall mutaiis mutandis apply to such kind of grain as they apply to wheat.
Therefore I move, seconded by the hon. member for Weyburn (Mr. McKay):
That subsection 2 of section 7 under section 4 of this bill, be struck out and the following substituted therefor:
The provisions of this act shall be made applicable to oats, barley, rye and flax, and shall, mutatis mutandis apply to such kind of grain as they apply to wheat.
Canadian Wheat Board Act

I think the minister should give an explanation of these two sections 7 and 8 under section 4 of the bill. I am bound to say that, without further information, I am rather opposed to this section because it gives altogether too much power to the government by order in council. Today our producers have no idea how their coarse grains may be handled during this coming crop year, and with that power there they may plant their grain and by order in council the price can be set, or they may have to market the grain for next to nothing at all. There is no provision there by statute, and at this date, so long after the termination of the war, it is a very bad piece of legislation. I hope the minister will give a further explanation as to why these sections are inserted. We should have that explanation before discussing the amendment.

With reference to this section, I suggest that if the handling of wheat is sound and acceptable generally to the farmers it is proper for the board to have authority from this house to handle all grains, including coarse grains such as rye, oats and barley, together with flax. This should be written into the act and that is the purpose of the amendment. If there are serious objections to the speculative handling of wheat, the same objections should hold with regard to the speculative handling of coarse grains and flax. I submit that it is essential to the economic well-being of producers of coarse grains that these grains be included in the operations of the board in order that a sound price relationship be established between the price of wheat and prices of coarse grains and flax. If a proper price relationship had existed between the prices of barley and wheat, it would not, in my opinion, be necessary to suggest that a bonus be paid in order to have increased production of barley.
There is still an improper relationship between the price of wheat and the price of rye. Trading in rye is being permitted on the exchange, and the amount of rye on paper last fall far outstripped the actual quantity of rye in existence for marketing purposes. Speculation was rife; the price of rye reaching heights which threw it out of all balance with wheat. The changing price relationship between wheat and rye is best illustrated by a study of the bulletin issued by the Department of Agriculture, statistics branch, in Saskatchewan. They show that in 1935 the price paid in Saskatchewan for wheat was sixty cents a bushel and for rye, twenty-five cents, whereas in 1946 the situation was reversed, wheat selling at SI.14 a bushel and rye at SI.96.

Either the price relationship in 1935 was wrong, or the relationship in 1946 was definitely out of balance. I suggest that the relationship in 1946 was definitely out of balance in comparison with that of 1935. It is not a sound price relationship, and in order to avoid such a situation being perpetuated, coarse grains and flax should be definitely included with wheat in the operations of the board. Therefore I support the amendment.

I should like to say a word with regard to the amendment that has been moved, and what I am going to say, I say as a result of considerable discussion with those who are interested. There is one member who I am sorry is not here because he has been more closely associated with those who have been dealing with the matter recently than most other members of the house. I refer to the hon. member for Swift Current. If the question involved is to be dealt with at all, I do not think it can be considered on as broad a basis as suggested by the hon. member for Yorkton.
The amendment, as I understand it, is intended to make this act apply to oats and barley and other grains in exactly the same way as it is now made to apply to wheat. I am quite certain that neither the farm organization nor the farmers generally would want the act to go quite that far, either those who agree with the government or those who disagree with the government. Wheat, as we grow it in w'estern Canada, is grown intentionally for the purpose of feeding human beings and is not utilized to any great extent by farmers as a feed, unless we grow a lower quality of it than we expect to, we intend to sell it largely outside the area in which it is grown. Therefore we set down a certain method of marketing it. Oats and barley, on the other hand-although this is not so true of rye-are grains which are grown largely for the purpose of feeding them on the farms where they are growm or of selling them from one farmer to another, or from one feeder to another within the area in which they are grown, which raises altogether different questions with regard to the marketing of the product.
If it were the desire of the committee to pass a provision such as the one suggested, that is if the committee decided that marketing of coarse grains could not be provided for by order in council, but that we must make this act apply in all ways to oats and barley, the same as it applies to wheat, you would be creating an undesirable situation. I do not think the farmers would want you to say that. Therefore I would suggest that this is not an amend-

Canadian Wheat Board Act
ment that ought to be passed in the words that have been suggested. The whole question would have to be given more consideration than we have given it before the committee should be prepared to accept the suggestion that coarse grains should be marketed in that way.
I have discussed the matter-and I do not think those with whom I have discussed it would object to my saying so-with those who market a considerable part of the grain of western Canada and have been very much interested in this type of legislation. I have never heard any of them suggest that oats and barley ought to be handled, even if the wheat board handles them, in the same manner as wheat is being handled. There would have to be a different system set up in order to have coarse grains handled by the board. What this does provide is that, if the government is convinced that coarse grains should be marketed under the wheat board, they may be so marketed. I may say that they are being marketed under the wheat board to a much greater degree than most of the discussion in this house has indicated; while the wheat board have not been handling coarse grains in just the same way as they have been handling wheat, there has not been very much done in the way of coarse grains in the last three or four years that has not been done pretty much under the control of the wheat board, and that may be the case for some time to come.
Someone passed a remark about participation. There has really been participation payment on oats and barley over the last two or three years made under the direction of the wheat board. The whole position in relation to coarse grains is so different from that in relation to wheat that I do not think you can deal with it by an amendment such as the one suggested. I would hope that the committee would accept the proposals in the bill as being in the best interests of Canada as a whole. We must remember a great deal of this coarse grain is shipped from western Canada to eastern Canada and to simply say that we are dealing only with this particular area which is covered by this bill would not be acceptable to the farmers of Canada. We should have to start all over again in drafting a bill dealing with the question if we are to have oats and barley marketed in anything like the same manner as we are proposing to handle wheat under this bill.

I think the minister was setting up straw men and knocking them down. He suggested that, if the amendment
of the hon. member for Yorkton carried, it would prevent local trading in coarse grains within the province.
No, I did not suggest that.
That was the inference I took from it.

No. What I am suggesting is that this bill in dealing with wheat applies to a certain designated area and the marketing of wheat from that designated area. You cannot purchase it in other than the designated areas. But it is largely marketed into other countries. As a matter of fact, the bill sets up that anywhere from one-third to one-half of the wheat going to market shall be marketed in Britain. I do not think you can apply that provision to oats and barley. Oats and barley are largely going to be fed in the area where they are grown and what is not fed there will largely be fed in the other parts of Canada. The farmers themselves would want a different method of handling grain for that purpose.

As I understand it, the main purpose of this bill is to take control of the marketing of wheat. Section 7, subsection 2, reads:
Except as directed by the governor in council, the board shall not buy grain, other than wheat.
The amendment which has been proposed would take that out and would leave the board with jurisdiction over those crops. As I understand it, what the government wants, with this amendment in there, is to be given the option of bringing those other crops under administration by the board. I think that is the intent of the legislation.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Not compulsorily.
No; to be given permission to bring them under the administration of the board.
Yes.

Members of the house and the country generally would like to have from the government, if they can get it, a statement as to what is seen in the future with respect to the taking over of the marketing of oats, barley, rye and flax. The government is now asking for power to take it over if they want to. Will they give us a full and frank statement as to the position they find themselves in, under what circumstances they might want to take it over, and what they might do.

Canadian Wheat Board Act
After Recess
The committee resumed at eight o'clock.

Mr. Chairman, shortly
before six o'clock, while speaking to the amendment moved by my colleague, the hon. member for Yorkton, the Minister of Agriculture made reference to the absence of my desk-mate and colleague, the hon. member for Swift Current. I, too, regret his unavoidable absence, but I would remind the minister that there are others of us who have had a considerable amount of experience in connection with farm organizations.
For the past twelve years or so I have not been allowed to be actively connected in an official position with these farm organizations because, as I have often said, in many of those farm organizations we lean over backwards to keep out of politics. It is for that reason I have not been able to take as active a part as I had been used to. I assure the minister, however, that I believe I can still speak from the experience I had during those earlier years.
Incidentally I may add that the years I spent in active participation in the activities of farm organizations were years to which I shall always look back as those spent among people who, whether they spoke English, French, German, Ukrainian or any other language, still spoke the same language because all of us were dealing with problems with which we were all familiar.
Speaking from that experience, and having assisted in the formation of some of the policies and programmes of farm organizations, I can say that throughout the years we have been opposed to speculations entering into the marketing of the products we produce on our farms. So that while the minister has referred to my desk-mate and colleague-and I along with the minister wish he were here tonight-I know that throughout the years when I sat in on the councils of our farm organizataions we laid down the policies, while others went out to inform our membership with respect to those policies.
I hold in my hand the 21st annual report of the Saskatchewan Cooperative Wheat Producers Limited. When the Minister of Agriculture was speaking to the amendment of the hon. member for Yorkton. if I remember correctly he made the statement that no farm organization had taken a definite stand with respect to having coarse grains brought in under the operations of the wheat board, to be handled in the same way as wheat is handled.

That was not my statement. But go on with your argument, and I shall clear the matter up later.
 .
If the minister remembers the wording of his statement I should prefer to have him state it now.

I hope I was not understood to have said that farm organizations are not in favour of having oats, barley and all other grains marketed under the wheat board. That is their definite view, and I believe they stated it in Winnipeg either yesterday or the day before, when they said that they want coarse grains handled by the wheat board. But my suggestion was that they do not want coarse grains handled by the wheat board in exactly the same way as that board is handling wheat.

That is right, but with this exception, that while sitting here listening to the minister, I believe I was not the on!}' one who gained the impression from what he said that farm organizations had not made a definite statement along that line.
I was not attempting to say that, if I did.

Along the lines of what the minister has just said, to the effect that they do not want to have coarse grains handled in identically the same way that wheat is handled by the wheat board, may I draw to his attention that that, I am sure, was not the intention of the hon. member for Yorkton when he moved the amendment. It will be recalled that our various types of grains come under the operations of the Canada Grain Act. We have different set-ups for different kinds of grain, and yet we have oats, barley and rye coming under that act, just as we have wheat, but have different regulations applying to the different kinds of grain.
Before the minister interrupted what I was saying, I was going to draw to his attention what is contained in the directors' report which appears in the 21st annual report of the Saskatchewan Cooperative Wheat Producers Limited. They state this:
For the post-war period your board believes (1) that the Canadian wheat board should continue to function as the sole marketing agency not only for wheat and flax as at present, but also for oats, barley and rye.
I hold in my hand a booklet entitled "U.F.C. Information," the official publication of the United Farmers of Canada, Saskatchewan section, dated April, 1946. This is one of the resolutions appearing in this publication:
Resolved that until producer organizations are in a position to take control of domestic and export marketing, we request that all grain be brought under the control of the Canadian wheat board, and that the name of said board be

Canadian Wheat Board Act
changed to the Canadian grain board, and that the board will be the sole marketing agency for all commercial grain;
Resolved that we are unalterably opposed to the reopening of any grain exchange in Canada.
Here is another quotation of a still later date from the same U.F.C. publication. This is dated October, 1946. I am sure the Minister of Agriculture is familiar with this, because it is a list of the proposals submitted to the government. Number 10 in the list is as follows:
The immediate abolition of the Winnipeg grain exchange.
I contend that when organized farmers see part of their grain used as a means for manipulative speculation, it has a detrimental effect on production and marketing. Consequently the reason I have risen is to correct any wrong impression which may have gone out from the minister's statement, and to reassure him and members of the committee that farmers want to have their grain marketed under the wheat board, or the grain board, whatever it may be called, without any manipulation from a speculative element.
I assure the minister that that is the view expressed not only in the resolutions and statements to which I have just referred but, from my personal experience, in every letter I get from my constituency in which the grain question is discussed, and in every resolution I receive from local farm organizations. All ask me to do everything I can to make it impossible for speculation again to become rampant in this country. I believe that is the wish of the great majority of producers in western Canada.
While my colleague, the hon. member for Yorkton, has offered an amendment to the section, may I point out that, so far as I am concerned, so long as the principle of that amendment is incorporated in the operations of the wheat board, I fully realize that we must have separate and somewhat different regulations from those pertaining to wheat.

I think the committee as a whole is indebted to the hon. member for Yorkton for moving the amendment he did this afternoon, because it brings into clear focus a question which has been disturbing my mind and, I am quite sure, the minds of many non-socialistic people in the Dominjon of Canada. I am bound to say in complete frankness that I do not like the legislation, but I am realist enough to know I cannot rise in my place and stop it. For a minute or two I intend to deal with the point raised by the amendment and, in fairness to myself, offer the opinion which I hold, and I believe this
to be the opinion of many liberal-minded people in this country, despite the oratory we have heard to the contrary.
The government which is sponsoring this bill has the opportunity to say whether the bill is in point of fact that which it purports to be, an expedient to permit the government to carry out the wheat contract which it has made, or whether it is, as the hon. member for Yorkton has suggested he hopes it is and as he has indicated he believes it to be, a declaration of faith in the socialist conception of marketing.

I never mentioned the socialist form of marketing.
Mr. MUTCH; I accept the hon. gentleman's correction with the best of grace. Two of them are honest about it, but the majority of the party which he represents never call it socialism. I do not care whether it is proposed by my hon. friend or by those in the government which I support, it is socialism and I do not like it any more on that account.

It is legislation brought in by your government.
Mr. MUTCH; Yes, and I do not like it any more than if you had brought it in, and for the same reason-it is socialist legislation. A little later on, when the proper section is reached I shall attempt to demonstrate that not only is it socialism in our time, it is socialism for ever. I do not want to be called to order and I shall leave that.
