The preamble of the bill states that the purpose of the act is to enable the government to carry out an agreement with the United Kingdom. If that is the purpose, then why has the government provided in the bill the opportunity to take power to include coarse grains? The hon. member for Selkirk and others are against that which they always describe as a gamble, the free marketing of this or any other commodity. Is this in point of fact the beginning of what my hon. friends obviously hope it is, an era of marketing on the socialist principle? I should- like an answer to that.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
What is the question? Was it whether this is a declaration of faith in socialism, or something?
Mr. MUTCH; I did not ask whether it was a declaration of faith in socialism; I stated that it was a principle of socialism as I see it. I should like some reason advanced for the inclusion of power to control coarse grains. I admit you are not taking that power and I expect that you will perhaps say you do not propose to take it, but I should like to know
Canadian Wheat Board Act

under what conditions you might conceivably take it and in what manner that can be reconciled with the declaration in the preamble that the purpose of the legislation is to carry out the wheat agreement.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
1 do not think the preamble says that that is the sole reason for the legislation. Apart altogether from what the preamble says, it may be desirable to support the coarse grains market as the Canadian wheat board has supported the w-heat market in the past. I hope every hon. member understands by this time that there is no power in this bill to compel anybody to deliver coarse grains to the Canadian wheat board at any time. The statements that have been made to the effect that there is power in this bill to extend the operations of the Canadian wheat board to coarse grains in the same way as it is to cover wheat during the next five years are incorrect. There is no power given to the Canadian wheat board to do anything except to buy coarse grains. There is no power conferred by this bill on the Canadian wheat board to compel anybody at any time to sell coarse grains to the government. That being the case, the suggestion of socialist principles in connection with the coarse grains feature of this bill is pretty far-fetched.
I am not interested in the argument, but it may be argued that when you pass an act by which all wheat going into interprovincial and export trade must be channeled through the Canadian wheat board you are putting the government in business in a very substantial way. People can apply any label they like to that departure, but there is no ground for placing the particular label that has been referred to on the provisions of this bill that deal with coarse grains. It does enable the Canadian wheat board to offer a fixed price, to put a floor under coarse grains; it does enable them to do that.

I had hoped that the information given would clarify the point as to whether there was that power in this legislation, power to take the exclusive purchase of coarse grains. I understand that that is not the case.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
That is not so and the
purpose of the amendment, as I understand it, is to put it there.
That is the answer I hoped to get.

I still am not clear
about this matter. As this section is drawn, it leaves it wide open for the government to take that power by order in council.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: To take what power?
The power to handle coarse grains.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: That was the cause of the interchange between the leader of the opposition and myself just before six o'clock. I thought he had the idea in his mind that the governor in council was taking power to compel every producer of coarse grains in Canada to sell his coarse grains through the wheat board for the purpose of interprovincial and export trade. We are not talcing that power. That is not contained anywhere in the bill.

I listened closely to what the Minister of Agriculture said before the dinner recess. I think he might have told us much more than he did. I appreciate that this bill is brought forth to provide for the carrying out of the wheat agreement with Great Britain, but we must not forget that we have other commitments with Great Britain and I am thinking mainly of the bacon agreement. That bacon agreement can be carried out only if some provision is made in connection with certain feed grains. That is not provided for in this bill. I do not want to prophesy or anything of that sort, but I think the Minister of Agriculture has something definite in his mind. It may not be according to the procedure of the committee, but if he would tell us what he has in mind it would be most helpful.
Provision must be made somehow for the production and sale of these coarse grains if we are to carry out to some degree that bacon contract. In the face of that, and because of the confusion that now exists in the minds of some of us in connection with these two clauses, I am going to ask the Minister of Trade and Commerce if he will let them stand for the time being until we get more information.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: What are the grounds for asking that they stand? There is no confusion in anybody's mind except in the minds of a few members of the opposition. We are not taking the power to have a monopoly on coarse grains.

Will the Minister of Justice tell me what power they are taking? Subsection 2 of the new section 7 reads:
Except as directed by the governor in council, the board shall not buy grain, other than wheat.
Except by order in council.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: That is right.

Does it not say that by order in council you may purchase these grains?

Canadian Wheat Board Act

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Exactly. This whole bill envisages the possibility that there may be an order in council authorizing the Canadian wheat board to buy coarse grains, but never compelling the delivery of grain, other than wheat, to the Canadian wheat board. In wheat, be it understood, the purpose of this legislation is that all wheat going into interprovincial and export markets must be channeled through the Canadian wheat board, but with regard to coarse grains no such power is contemplated or authorized by this bill. The only thing that can be done with regard to coarse grains under this bill is that the Canadian wheat board may be authorized by the governor in council to purchase coarse grains.

Would the Minister of Agriculture care to say anything further which might enlighten us in this connection? I know he has something further in mind in order to carry out other agreements, and while it might not be in order under the procedure we are following, it would be helpful because these things are all tied together.

I have been looking for an opportunity to say something without being out of order in doing so. All I can say at the moment is that I think it is quite proper for us to take the position that, before we can say anything more with regard to coarse grains or other farm products, as at least a matter of courtesy we ought to hear the Canadian Federation of Agriculture tomorrow. Before they held their annual meeting in Winnipeg they asked for a date when they might meet the government to present their views on the question of coarse grains and other farm products. No day could be set earlier than February 28, which is tomorrow, for the federation to meet the government. Tomorrow they are coming to present their case. After they have done so and we have heard their argument, we shall announce the policy in relation to feed grains, just as soon as we can have it evolved as a result of hearing what they have to say. But tonight I would hesitate even to forecast what might be the result of that consideration and those discussions tomorrow.
That might be a good reason for letting this section stand. I do not believe we can complete this bill tonight.
I hardly believe this would affect it.
In view of the discussion that has taken place, I wonder if the hon. member would care to withdraw his amendment?
That is about the last thing I would do. It is my intention to carry on.

I should like to say a few words on the amendment. The hon. member for Winnipeg South should have accepted the invitation extended to members of this house to sit in and listen to the discussions taking place at the meeting of the Canadian Federation of Agriculture at the Chateau Laurier yesterday, with regard to the marketing of farm products. If he had done so he might have had a different point of view from that which he seems to have today. The Canadian Federation of Agriculture by no means can be called a socialistic organization; yet in their discussions yesterday not one man raised any objection to the controlled marketing of farm products, and when I say "controlled marketing" I mean compulsory marketing, where over fifty per cent, or a given percentage of the producers of the agricultural product in question want it marketed by a board. As the minister has stated, they are going to present a brief to the government with respect to the orderly marketing of farm products, and I expect coarse grains will be included. After listening to the discussions yesterday, I shall be very much surprised if they do not recommend that the government take over the marketing of all coarse grains, if not under this act, then under similar legislation.
Just before the dinner recess, the Minister of Agriculture was building up straw men and knocking them down, as to what the amendment moved by the hon. member for Yorkton might do with regard to the marketing of coarse grains within a province. The wheat board does not interfere with the marketing, within a province, of wheat for seed or feed. That can be carried on quite freely, and the same would apply to coarse grains. I suggest, too, that the Minister of Agriculture and the Minister of Justice should get together, because we have had from them two quite different statements. Before the dinner recess, the Minister of Agriculture stated1 that coarse grain marketing in this country was controlled by the wheat board to a far greater extent than many hon. members seemed to realize. Then after the dinner recess, the Minister of Justice said that it was not proposed to control the marketing of coarse grains to the extent that the marketing of wheat is controlled.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
There is no contradiction whatever.

Canadian Wheat Board Act

There may not be, but at least the impression of a contradiction was left in my mind. I am quite sure that the amendment moved by the hon. member for Yorkton would meet with the approval of the great majority of the farmers in the designated areas under this bill. As the hon. member for Humboldt stated, their organizations have persistently and consistently, over the last number of years, asked that coarse grains should be controlled and marketed in a manner similar to that under which wheat is marketed by the wheat board. No one says that this should be done in exactly the same way; the amendment moved does not suggest that. Special circumstances that might arise in connection with the marketing of those grains could be dealt with by regulation. I am quite sure it could be done. Therefore we do not intend to withdraw this amendment. We believe it is the right thing to do, and we intend to see that a vote is taken on it.

The leader of the opposition asked a question earlier in the day, or asked a question yesterday which was answered today. He put the direct question to the Minister of Justice as to whether we had consulted the legal authorities and what their opinion was as to whether this legislation was intra vires. This afternoon the Minister of Justice read the reply, to the effect that the government considered the legislation intra vires or it would not have been introduced in the house. This question is involved in the advice which was received, and I am sure anyone who is an authority on the question will agree that if we were to attempt to force the handling of coarse grains, as they are and must be marketed in Canada, to be under the same terms that we have provided for wheat in this bill, we would be endangering the whole measure, not only as it relates to coarse grains, but as it relates to wheat and everything else in it. I think everyone would agree to that.
As a matter of fact quite accidentally I had an opportunity, since speaking here this afternoon, to talk with those who are in authority in connection with the farm movement in western Canada. That came about because they called me, not because I called them. I want to repeat what I said before the dinner recc-ss, that I have discussed this question with representatives of the organizations in western Canada on many occasions, and on no occasion have they ever maintained that coarse grains held the same relationship to the authority of this house in dealing with legislation of this kind as does wheat. And while they have passed resolution after resolution-and passed a resolution no later than 
this week-asking this government to try to find some way to have all grains placed under the wheat board, they realize, as everyone who has made a study of this question does, that there is a difference.
We have had that difference indicated in many other farm products. I do not object at all to the hon. member for Melfort, or any other hon. member, who believes in the idea of having coarse grains handled exactly as wheat is handled, presenting his point of view to the committee; but I am afraid that before the committee would be in a position to put coarse grains, as they must be marketed in Canada, in exactly the same position as wheat, under the wheat board, it would be necessary for us to have an amendment to the constitution. I am not saying that we should not have such an amendment; probably we should, but up to the present we do not have it; and, not having it, I am afraid that if we were to introduce into this legislation the suggestion that is made in the amendment we would be endangering the legislation as a whole.
There may be some hon. members who would say that that is the quickest way to get rid of the whole thing, but I hope that is not the position taken by those who want this type of marketing to have a fair trial. If the committee wishes to take a vote on the legislation as it is I would suggest that hon. members take that into consideration when they are voting.
The appeal that I made before the dinner recess was not to ask the hon. member for Yorkton to refrain from moving his amendment; the appeal I made to him was to check the amendment which I have not before me but which I understand meant what I thought it meant. The amendment has now been placed in my hands and it reads as follows:
Moved by Mr. Castleden, seconded by Mr. McKay, that subsection 2 of section 7 of this bill be struck out and the following substituted therefor:	"The provisions of this act shall be
made applicable to oats, barley, rye and flax, and mutatis mutandis apply to such kind of grain as they apply to wheat.
As I said before the dinner recess, this amendment has as its objective that all grains be handled under the wheat board in the same way that we have suggested in this bill wheat should be handled. I submit again that to do that would place the legislation in danger of being declared ultra vires. To carry out the idea that the hon. member for Yorkton has in mind, I think it would be much better to leave the bill in its present form. There is nothing in the bill as it now stands to prevent farm organizations from coming and saying that oats and barley should be brought

___________ Canadian Wheat Board Act
under the wheat board, not by compulsion, but by the board saying that they are prepared to pay more for oats and barley than anyone else is prepared to pay under the conditions which exist, and thereby get control of oats and barley in order to utilize it for any purpose such as a greater production of hogs or anything else that we may have in mind. There is nothing in the bill as it now stands to prevent that from being done; there is nothing in the bill to prevent farm organizations from asking us to do that and insisting on our doing that, but I do wish to say-

The minister says that there is nothing in the bill to prevent certain things from happening. Under the terms of the bill, there is nothing to prevent the minister by order in council from authorizing the purchase of some of these commodities on the Winnipeg grain exchange.

I am sure that the hon. member for Humboldt will agree with me when I say that if we wanted to make it absolutely certain that we would have no authority to do it we would not put it in the bill at all. That is all we would need to have done to place our position before the committee as being that of not desiring to have anything whatever to do with the marketing of oats and barley. We could have left this provision entirely out of the bill, but we have placed in the bill a provision which does empower the government to handle oats and barley and any other grain if they desire to do so. I think that is as far as the committee should ask us to go at this time. We shall have experience with this legislation and we may have occasion to do certain things with the constitution as we go along, but for the time being, because of the constitution as it is, and because of the representations which have been made to us at the present time, we are going in this bill as far as we can be expected to go.

I wish to reply to some of the remarks made by the Minister of Agriculture with regard to the constitutional question. When I listened to the Minister of Justice this afternoon explaining his position and the position of the government on the constitutional question I wholly agreed with him. I believe the government is absolutely within its rights in having this bill passed. The board is incorporated with the object of marketing in an orderly manner, in interprovincial and export trade, grain grown in Canada. According to the definition of the bill, "grain" means oats, barley, rye, flax and flaxseed. If the contention of the Minister of Agriculture is right and if we try to buy and 83166-55
sell coarse grains under this legislation it would be ultra vires. It is ultra vires already and what the minister told us this afternoon is not so, if the Minister of Agriculture is right, although I am of the opinion that the Minister of Justice's interpretation of the law which he gave this afternoon is correct. I cannot see in the bill anything which would make it unconstitutional if the amendment were adopted.
Subsection 2 of the proposed section 7 makes it optional for the governor in council to deal in grains other than wheat. All that the motion of the hon. member for Yorkton does is to make it compulsory, so to speak, if you wish to use that word. So far as the constitutional question is concerned, I cannot see anything in the explanation of the Minister of Agriculture.

So far as this group
is concerned, the last thing we would wish to do would be to jeopardize in any possible way the bill in relation to its handling of wheat. Just as quickly as the government can show us how it is affected constitutionally, and under what grounds, we shall have to come to terms; but I should like to point out to the Minister of Justice that there must have been some change in the constitution since 1935. I should like to refer him to section 14 of the original act which was passed in 1934 and which reads as follows:
The governor in council may approve of the provisions of this act being made applicable to oats, barley, rye or flax produced in the provinces of Manitoba, Saskatchewan, Alberta and British Columbia, if the board recommends that such approval be given, whereupon the provisions of this act shall mutatis mutandis apply to such kind of grain as they apply to wheat.
The wording is almost identical with the amendment now before the committee.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
My hon. friend must surely
see that the act was a voluntary act. That was an act under which the government were not compelling anybody to sell anything to them. They were offering to buy wheat, and they were then providing that they might offer to buy coarse grains as well. But now we are doing a new type of thing in the legislation which is before the committee. In fact we are endeavouring to enact provisions under which the wheat which is produced in this designated area, if it goes into interprovincial and export trade, must go through the Canadian wheat board. That is a matter of compulsion, and we have to be sure of the constitutionality of such a move. For the reasons which I gave this afternoon, wheat being mainly an export commodity, largely an export commodity, pre-

Canadian Wheat Board Act

dominantly an export commodity, we think we keep within the confines of our constitutional powers when we deal with wheat. But the law officers tell me that the situation would be much more doubtful when you are dealing with commodities which are predominantly sold in Canada. Take a commodity three-quarters of which is sold in Canada or within the provinces-where will you stop your operations in that case?
When it reaches the point where it goes outside the province.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
Will your operations be
effective if you deal with a quarter of the commodity in that way, and what quarter will you deal with?

You will deal with more
than a quarter of the coarse grains in western Canada. I think you will find that a larger percentage than a quarter goes into trade other than within the province. I do not know what the figures are, but the amendment offered by the hon. member for Yorkton deals with coarse grains the same as wheat and in the bill you deal only with wheat that is used between the provinces or for export. His amendment would simply mean that the coarse grains which were sold extra-provincially or outside Canada for export would come under the act the same as wheat. I have never yet seen in the constitution anything that declared that, so far as the dominion government is concerned, it is unconstitutional for it to handle a product of which seventy five per cent remains in the province and twenty-five per cent goes out. No percentages are mentioned in the British North America Act which would make it either constitutional or unconstitutional for the product to be handled on the basis of the amount that goes into export or the amount that remains in the province, and I cannot see how it will affect the constitutionality of the act. I can see how it might affect the effectiveness of handling coarse grains if too small a percentage were controlled by the board, but in the case of grains from designated areas, there is I believe a sufficient amount of these going into the trade outside the provinces to justify their being placed under the act.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
I am afraid I cannot argue the point very well. All I can say is, I am told that the constitutional objections in the case of commodities which are not mainly export commodities, largely export commodities or commodities moving into interprovincial trade, are very much more serious than in the case of wheat. There are, I am told, cases in con-

nection with wheat as mainly export trade. But you cannot be too mathematical about the matter, because the courts will look at the real pith and substance of what you are trying to do, and if you try to reach out and control that which is essentially a domestic commodity, or a commodity a large proportion of the transactions of which are in the province, you are getting outside your field. That is what I am told. I am sorry I cannot make a better or more convincing argument on it but that is my information. Apart altogether from that, however, I may say that personally I doubt whether it would be wise to do it, though that is for other people than myself to say.
It seems to me, from the statements we have had from two ministers-
Three ministers.

Two anyway. From the statements we have had from them, it seems that no one knows whether we are in the barley business or the coarse grain business or whether we shall ever be, and that is why the members of this party, myself in particular, would like to have a statement from the Minister of Trade and Commerce. I suggest that he take tonight to think it over so that he can tell us tomorrow what the government will do with barley, what they can do with it, what they intend to do with it, or whether they are going to do anything at all with it. They say it is unconstitutional. It may be, but the department, through the regulations, has been handling coarse grains to a large extent and is doing so at the present time.
Under the War Measures Act.

Under the War Measures Act and under the regulations passed by virtue of that act. They have been doing it, and the objection to putting in the act an authority such as this which is asked for in section 7, subsection 2, so far as I can make out, is this. We do not know what system is to be followed in handling it. The Minister of Justice says they are taking authority to buy, but if you take authority to buy you must intend to sell. We do not know and we have no way of finding out. From any of the statements made up to date we have not been able to get any light on the subject. If you take over barley, how will you do it? Will you give participation certificates, or what will you do? Before we are asked to give the power to handle coarse grains, the committee should be told what the government have in mind. If they have nothing in mind, then leave it out and change the definition of "grain". But surely, when they cannot tell us what they are

Canadian Wheat Board Act
going to do, when they do not know what powers they have to do it, they cannot ask us to give them the power to do something in such a nebulous form, and by order in council. That is one of the objections I have.
I would judge from what has just been said that the hon. member is not in favour of the amendment. That is what is before the committee. Is he in favour of it or not?
I am not prepared to say at the moment, because apparently three ministers who should know more than I do-and I am a new member-cannot make up their minds what they will do.
That is not correct. Three ministers have definitely stated that they are against it.

What we should like to know from the Minister of Trade and Commerce is his intended plan of handling barley and coarse-grains if he does handle them. Surely to goodness he can tell us that, and if he cannot tell us tonight, then we suggest that the amendment stand and that consideration of the amendment moved by the member for York-ton should also stand, and tomorrow the minister can tell us where the government stands.
Mr. MaeINNIS: If this amendment comes to a vote I shall have to vote on it. Consequently I should like to know where I stand before I do that. As the hon. member for Yorkton has said, the last thing we want to do is to jeopardize this legislation. The amendment seeks, if I understand it correctly, to bring buying and selling of coarse grains under the wheat board. I believe that is the purpose of it. Subsection 2 of section 7 on page 6 of the bill states that the governor in council may authorize the board to buy grain other than wheat. I should like the Minister of Justice to tell me in what way that differs from the power that is asked by the amendment. If it is illegal under the amendment; if the amendment and this section mean exactly the same thing, that is, the buying and selling of grain by the wheat board, then it seems strange to me that it should be ultra vires when it is done by a section in the act and intra vires when it is done by order in council. It does not seem real, but perhaps I am not seeing it correctly and I should like an explanation by the minister.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
The difference is this. Under the act the Canadian wheat board may be empowered, if the necessary order in council is passed, to buy and sell grain. There cannot be anything ultra vires about that. That is simply a Canadian corporation being 83166-55i
empowered to buy and sell a particular commodity. There is no compulsion exercised upon the seller of the commodity to sell it. But what is proposed by the amendment is that there be a compulsion upon every seller of coarse grains, who is selling into interprovincial or export trade, to sell it to the Canadian wheat board. When you undertake to do that-and we have undertaken to do it and are doing it in this bill with reference to wheat-you must be very careful that you do not trespass upon the field of property and civil rights. When you exercise compulsion upon a man, prima facie his civil rights are being affected, and you must be sure you have power to do that.
What is the difference between the rights of a wheat grower and the rights of an oat grower?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: If we were to put the government into the business of compelling growers of coarse grains to deliver their coarse grain to the wheat board, you would have either effective control or ineffective control. It may be possible for the wheat board to operate in a careful, ineffective manner in commodities such as coarse grains and yet operate constitutionally. But if they were to handle substantially the whole, or a very large proportion of the volume of coarse grain-which, I suppose, they would have to do if the operations were to be effective-I am told that their acts would likely be unconstitutional.

As chairman of the committee I think I have a responsibility to draw to the attention of the members the question of the validity of this amendment. It is a well known rule that no private member can move an amendment which would involve the expenditure of money. This is a point I was hoping some hon. member would speak on in order that I could get the opinion of the committee. I think the amendment is out of order.
You have not as yet, Mr. Chairman, ruled the amendment out of order.
He is just creeping up on it.

In regard to the matter of constitutionality, I should like to say, as has been stated before, that we do not wish to endanger the bill. However, if there is anything in the constitution of this country which prevents the farmers, through their organizations, from marketing their products to the best advantage, then I say it is time we changed the constitution. I believe this committee would approve that, and I would sug-
Canadian Wheat Board Act

gest to the government that any changes that are necessary should be instituted at this session of parliament. The organized farmers today realize that orderly marketing of their products is absolutely essential. We all remember the experience after the last war with regard to agricultural products and what happened in connection with the speculative market. If the constitution of this country is such that the people cannot do as they want to do, we ought to change it.

I just wish to say a word because I want to make myself plain. Speaking quite personally, I am opposed to the amendment, whether it be in order or out of order. The reason this bill is brought forward now with its compulsory features in connection with wheat is as a result of the agreement with Britain, and let me say that I support it for the reason that our government, elected by our people, signed the document and we are going to see to it that it is carried out. I do not like the agreement, but that is water over the dam or under the bridge,- or wherever water goes. But I want to make it plain that I am totally opposed, except for the agreement with Britain, to this government forcing the farmer to sell his goods to A, B, C, or D, whether you call it the wheat board or whether you do not.
There is another thing I wish to ask the government, and I think it has been fairly put to them by my hon. friends to my immediate left. I think the government should be as frank as I am. Do they favour the compulsory handling of coarse grain by a wheat board? I have heard the ministers talk all around or over the question.
Mr. ILSLEY I cannot speak on behalf of the government, but I will say that, personally, I am not.

May I say that I heard the answer of the Minister of Justice with the greatest of delight. I was sure he would say that. Now that we are holding this evangelistic meeting, there are two more ministers for us to hear from.

Even in a revival meeting I do not usually go very far beyond the present time. I wish to say that I am opposed to putting the compulsory clause as related to coarse grains into this bill, which is what we are dealing with at the present time. I am opposed to that, and I think that is about as far as one needs to go at the moment.

I have listened to the statement made by the Minister of Agriculture, and am inclined to think he

is not a convert. He is only beginning his moral rearmament. WThat his answer means is that tonight he is not in favour. He twitted me the other evening about being unable to make up my mind on a certain matter, but I cannot discuss that because that section does not come in here. It seems to me that the Minister of Agriculture of the Dominion of Canada should be able to tell this committee w'hether or not he is in favour of the compulsory marketing of coarse grains through a wheat board, and as yet he has failed to do that. So that we now turn to the last sinner who may repent, the Minister of Trade and Commerce. I have known him so long that I appreciate those eloquent silences of his very much. He, like the Minister of Agricu-ture, may want to change his mind after the session ends when we have no chance to say anything to him.
Coming to the legal aspect of it, may I say that I am not much of a lawyer, and I know that-

Oh, yes, you are.
Mr. SMITH (Calgary West)but I agree with my barber shop lawyer friends to my left that you cannot make a distinction between twenty-five per cent being exported and seventy-five per cent being exported. I know of no legal principle-although there are many of those principles which I do not know -which will support any other position. So I conclude by saying that I support the principle of this bill, because I know the wheat to meet our obligations cannot be obtained unless some control is exercised over it; but I give my support only because of that agreement. I am unalterably opposed to that authority being extended to the handling of any other farm product. Somebody is going to say that I represent a city constituency. I have in my constituency about one hundred polls, of -which about forty are ih the country. I hope the papers publish what I have said, because I am anxious to meet my farmer friends on exactly the basis I have suggested to this committee tonight.

The hon. member for Calgaty West made the statement, "I am not in favour of the compulsory marketing of grain". When he made that statement there was a good deal of applause not only from this side of the house, but from the other side as well.
I want to tell hon. members of this House of Commons, no matter what party they are in, that I heard farmers from all parts of Canada speak in the Chateau Laurier yesterday, and I was surprised to hear some of the representatives of farmers in that meeting

__________ Canadian Wheat Board Act
say that they were not afraid of compulsion, that they had tried a voluntary system of marketing for years, that it had been a failure, and that today they were going out asking for compulsory marketing not only of wheat, not only of coarse grains, but of potatoes, apples and all the other farm products of Canada. And if the present members in the House of Commons are not alive enough to see the trend that is going across Canada today, they will soon be replaced by different members.

I am not satisfied that it will be in the interests of western farmers to place coarse grains in this bill. I have in mind, of course, especially Alberta. I cannot speak for the farmers of Saskatchewan. The difficulty we of this group are in at the present time is that we do not know what the government's coarse grains policy is. For the last three weeks we have been asking the government to declare its policy with respect to coarse grains. So far, that policy has not been declared, and therefore we do not know what the situation is.
On the other hand, we do know that the situation as between wheat and coarse grains is entirely different. Wheat is on an export market basis, and to a large extent coarse grains are on a domestic market. In our part of the country one of our main difficulties has been, not to sell coarse grains but to obtain enough coarse grains to feed the stock we have. But there is danger that if coarse grains are put in the wheat board bill coarse grains can be drained out of the province and we would be short. We should like to have provincial control of coarse grains because we seldom have enough.
So far as the price of coarse grains is concerned, it is my experience that, so long as the wheat price is maintained at a high level, the price of coarse grains will stay up. When the price of wheat goes up the farmers no longer feed wheat, but feed coarse grains instead, and that helps coarse grains to stay up in price. Therefore I do not believe it will pay to put coarse grains under this bill, so long as we are on a domestic market basis.
But if in future we produce coarse grains to the extent that we export a large volume, then the situation might be different, and it might pay to put them under the bill.

I have listened to the hon. member for Melfort and again to the hon. member for The Battlefords tonight say that they attended the meeting of the Canadian Federation of Agriculture in Ottawa yesterday. I also attended that meeting yesterday. Although my interpretation of what the
farmers in this country want may be wrong- and I have been wrong before, and I expect I may be wrong again-it was my interpretation of what they want; and although it may be wishful thinking on the part of our hon. friends to the left, it is not government control of marketing that they want, but enabling legislation by which they can control their own markets.

Having listened to the hon. member for Brant, may I say I think he will find, when the recommendations are presented to the government, that he will be wrong once more, because the matter was thoroughly discussed at that meeting, and the opinion of the meeting was apparently unanimous that, while farmers now had the right themselves to control the marketing of farm products within a province, that was not enough. They want the government to have an act passed setting up a dominion marketing board, with members appointed by the government.
The draft bill which the farmers had before them yesterday-and I have a copy of it with me now-stated, with regard to the appointment of a marketing board, that the board shall consist of such number of persons as the governor in council may from time to time determine, and each member shall hold office during pleasure and receive such remuneration as the governor in council may determine.
That is the government board. Certainly that is what they are asking for, because this is the draft bill they had before them yesterday.
Does the hon. member suggest that the board that the Canadian Federation of Agriculture is asking for would consist of government employees and government men, not producers?
I read the section from the draft bill. It is quite clear, and if the hon. member cannot understand it I cannot do anything for him.

I, too, was at the meeting of the Canadian Federation of Agriculture yesterday. I, too, have a copy of the bill, and it has the purpose and intention as stated. I can say the federation of agriculture represents not only wheat, but cheese, asparagus, potatoes, sugar beets-the whole ambit of agricultural commodities. The provincial act merely covers the production of grain and marketing within the province. The thing they want is that the government should step in and take the other segment-interprovincial and export trade- and pass legislation which would integrate all marketing for the whole of the Dominion of Canada.
Canadian Wheat Board Act

That is the purport and intent set out in the bill.
The purpose and intent is to provide, in respect of interprovincial trade in Canada and in export trade, for the improvement of the methods and practices of marketing of natural products, and for the promotion, control, regulation or prohibition of the marketing of natural products, in any or all respects and in whole or in part.
And the delegates said that again and again and again. While the opinion expressed in one part of the house was expressed at that meeting, I think it was a Tory opinion, and it had the usual flavour of opposing something that is good for the majority. Again and again these organizations got up and said that ninety per cent of the growers wanted something but that ten per cent went out and spoiled the whole picture for the ninety per cent. They went out and made contracts which simply ruined the whole price structure-just played it with deuces wild, and spoiled the whole thing.
Again and again they expressed the futility of voluntary organization. After all, there is a principle of democracy involved here. If the people of this country have a chance to elect a government on a principle, a chance to defeat a government, it is not undemocratic for that government to pass a law enabling the majority of producers to handle their product, and to make it compulsory. After all, are not our traffic laws compulsory? Is not taxation compulsory? Is not education compulsory? I may not keep my children out of school, because the people of this country realize that we cannot afford ignorance. And we cannot afford ignorance in marketing, either.
During the last dominion election we heard all these things advocated, controls of everything, but let me say-
Oh, oh.
Hear, hear.
I hope hon. members will not interrupt the hon. member when he is speaking. They are supposed to be gentlemen and I hope they will act accordingly.

Members of the C.C.F. to my left advocated controls during the last election; but, speaking for the county of Simcoe, which I represent, let me say that they were told in no uncertain terms by the people that they did not want controls.
My hon. friend represents only a part of the county of Simcoe.

My hon. friend is quite correct, but I repeat that Simcoe county

declared itself regarding government controls even if it did elect one Liberal. The men responsible for producing the finest oats in North America and the finest apples in Canada live in Simcoe county. The farmers and other citizens of Simcoe county do not want controls, on grain or any other commodity.

I should like to say one word in connection with the argument between the hon. member for Brant and the hon. member for Melfort. The hon. member for Melfort should be well acquainted with Renfrew North because he campaigned there.
I suggest to the hon. member that if he comes into Renfrew North and advocates that the marketing of farm products should be compulsory he will meet with as little success as he did in the 1945 election campaign in that constituency.

In my opinion this amendment is so clearly out of order that I feel it my duty and obligation to rule it out of order. It is well known that no private member can move an amendment which will involve expenditures and, as I see it, this amendment contravenes the well known rule of parliament that no charge against the people can be entertained without the previous recommendation of the governor general. If the Minister of Agriculture brings in a bill later he will do that on his own responsibility as a minister of the crown. The present amendment has been moved by a private member and since, in my opinion, it will involve expenditures, I must rule it out of order.

Speaking to the point of order, I submit that the amendment will not cost the government anything, nor will it necessitate the expenditure of funds. The wheat board act states clearly that as soon as the boards-
Order.
I have given my ruling. It is the best I can do, but I think I am right.
May I submit that, before a ruling is handed down, an opportunity should be given to those who believe it is in order to discuss the amendment.

I do not think the hon. member was in the chamber when I raised that point in the hope that someone would speak to it. No one spoke to it and I feel it my duty and responsibility as chairman to rule the amendmentout of order.

Section agreed to.

Canadian Wheat Board Act
On section 5.

When I spoke a few minutes ago I indicated that when we came to section 5 I would have something more to say. This section introduces a new part II into the bill to replace sections 12 to 18 of the previous act which are to be repealed. A few moments ago I said that, in my opinion, the bill represented socialism in our time and that on another clause I would suggest that it perpetuated that condition. The stated purpose of part II is to apportion elevator and transportation facilities equitably amongst producers, but it goes far beyond that. As I understand it, if the board wishes to exercise its power it may control the whole grain industry in a fashion even more absolute than that which is provided for in part IV, which merely forbids private export or interprovincial trade for a limited time.
The new section 13, which is part of section 5, indicates that power is taken to forbid the movement of grain, the delivery of grain and the use of facilities for the movement of grain except with the permission of the board. The explanatory note reads:
The purpose of the control is to apportion the use of elevator and transportation facilities equitably amongst producers.
The provisions of the new section 13 and the subsequent sections-these must all be considered together-especially subsection 4 of section 15, effectively give the board the power absolutely to control the grain industry in a designated area. In part IV we have an expression of the intention of the bill, that it is to permit the fulfilment of the wheat agreement. In that part there is a limitation placed upon the powers which are to be exercised.
I wish to point out what I meant when I said that this is permanent socialism, if you accept my definition for that. As I understand it, there is no provision for the termination of the powers granted by part II of this bill, whatever the intent of the sponsors of the bill may be. As I read it, the meaning is that power is taken to do all that part IV does, at a time when part IV shall have lapsed, unless the government is prepared to agree that the limitation clause, which is section 29 of part IV, shall be applied to the powers taken under part II. It is literally true that part II gives control over the industry which is not even attempted in part IV. We recognize the constitutional limitations in part IV, the part of the bill designed to carry out the wheat agreement, but in part II we forget about those limitations and, under the guise of controlling elevator and transportation facilities, we control in minute detail what
has been, and what conceivably may be again, at such time as section 29 becomes operative, private enterprise in this country.
When I was on my feet previously I said I had no expectation of being able to convert either the government or those who support them so loyally on this bill, and I am not hypocrite enough to suggest that I am leading a crusade for a forlorn hope. I am sincere, however, in desiring to point out to this committee that, whatever may be the intention if part II of the bill is carried in its present form there is danger that we may give to the board power, under another guise, to do the very things this bill proposes the board shall renounce, under part IV, at the expiration of this agreement with England. Consequently I should like an expression from the government as to whether or not they would be willing to consider introducing into part II the limiting section of part IV, in whatever terms that section may finally be accepted by the house, and so terminating the powers being taken to oontrol the industry through the control of elevator and transportation facilities and even of deliveries to mill, because by definition mills are included in the act. I should like to know whether the government will consider such a limitation in part II. If they will not consider such a limitation, then I should like an explanation as to why these powers are considered necessary. I have not consulted any of the gentlemen concerned, but in view of the experience they have had I would be surprised if the wheat board itself either expected or needs the perpetuation of the powers granted in part II.
I foresee a time when we may be back in the position of having both private trade and a wheat board in existence in Canada. The Minister of Agriculture indicated the other day, I think, that he did not look forward to such a dual position, with the wheat board left holding the bag in tough times and the trade carrying on and getting most of the business in normal times. That is beside the point, perhaps, but I cannot envisage such a situation arising provided these limitations are put in part II. If part II remains as it is, however, I can see where in law it might be possible to return to private enterprise the marketing of farm products, and at the same time have the wheat board continue to carry on with power to control elevators and transportation, which would permit the wheat board, if it so desired, to make the legal situation, in fact, completely ridiculous and ineffective. I am not suggesting that the present wheat board is likely to exercise those powers in future, but I should like to know
Canadian Wheat Board Act

first why they are considered necessary, and, second, if we may not expect the same limitation on these extraordinary powers in part II which the bill itself proposes to impose in part IV.
If I understood what the hon. member for Winnipeg South was driving at, it was that these powers given to the board should end at a given date, approximating the end of the British agreement?
Not later than that.

But we are already negotiating other agreements. The British agreement is just a step in the direction the organized farmers of this country want to go in the marketing and exporting of their products. Today in another part of the world we have a meeting of people who are trying to draft an international agreement to make this multilateral, and the suggestion is that it go on for five years from 1947. That would take it into 1952, and any action on the part of this government to curtail this act to 1950, in the face of the negotiations going on, I think would be a means of destroying those negotiations, which the organized farmers and wheat growers of western Canada have been fighting for during the past ten years.

Is the hon. gentleman
announcing government policy?
No; I am giving the policy of - this party, and thank goodness the hon. gentleman's party has seen fit to adopt some of it.

I wonder if we would not make more progress now in dealing with section 5 if we take these subclauses as they come. We are dealing with section 12 of section 5. Shall section 12 carry?
Section 5 (section 12) agreed to.
On section 5 (section 13)-Conditions for delivery of grain to elevator.

I should like to ask the minister about deliveries to elevators, and I have taken this matter up previously with both the wheat board and the Minister of Trade and Commerce. If you deliver grain to a town where there are five or six elevators you have the privilege of delivering to any elevator you wish. If you live where there is only one elevator you may only deliver to that elevator, although there may be another one three miles away. I think that is very unfair, because if you are at a small point where there is only one elevator, you may have some difficulty or there may be some bad feeling between you and the elevator agent.

If you live where there are six elevators you can overcome that difficulty; you can drive past his door and go to the next elevator, which is quite legal under the act. I am not going to move any amendlment, but in fairness to the western farmer I say he should have the right to go to the next elevator if he wants to.
He has that right.
No, he has not.
I am informed that if the producer in question writes to the Canadian wheat board at Winnipeg, pointing out that situation, he will be given that right to change his delivery point.

Perhaps I have not made myself quite clear. If there are six elevators alongside each other at Dauphin or at some other point, a farmer's permit book allows him to go to any of those elevators at any time. He does not need to sign up for any particular elevator. But if he has a point like Millbrook with one elevator, and he signs for that elevator, he cannot go anywhere else. If there is an elevator at Dugald and the farmer goes there, he cannot come back to the other elevator. He has not the privilege of going to two elevators.
That is compulsion. That is what you want, is it not?
No; we only want a square deal.
I am advised that the Canadian wheat board will give any producer that right at any time, upon application.
But he cannot use two; he can only use one.
Oh, no, he cannot have two delivery points.

Then why give him six if there are that many elevators in a town? If he delivers to a point where there are six elevators he can go to any one he likes with his permit book. When he has a choice between two points, each having one elevator, he must swear allegiance to either one or the other for that season.
Or some other elevator close by.
No; he can go to only one.

I am very glad to find that the hon. member for Selkirk is a little bit individualistic and anti-socialist as far as the delivery of his own grain is concerned. I think that shows a little hope that the C.C.F. party may progress toward reasonable ways of thinking.

Canadian Wheat Board Act
However, actually I wanted to ask a question about paragraph (c) of this section. The first part of this section states:
Except with the permission of the board, no person shall deliver grain to an elevator, and no manager or operator thereof shall receive delivery of grain unless
(c) the grain was produced in the crop year in which delivery is made on the lands described in the permit book or in any other crop year on any lands whatsoever.
The first part of paragraph (c) seems to say that only grain will be delivered which was grown on the land described in the permit book in that particular year. The second part of it seems to say just the reverse. Will the minister explain exactly what the paragraph means? As it stands, I am not able to make any sense out of it.

Mr. Chairman, will you permit me to answer the hon. member very quickly? He is talking about my selling grain. Since I have come to this country, I have learned never to market grain except through hogs or cattle. I have not been the victim of the speculators.
I am glad the hon. member has compassion for his friends.
This paragraph deals with a person who moves from one piece of land which he is farming to another. If he brings any grain with him from the land which he was first on he may also market that grain.

This paragraph says: "... or in any other crop year on any lands whatsoever." Did I understand the minister to say that this applies only to a farmer who has moved from his original holding to another holding? If so, it should be so specified in the paragraph. If it means something else I should like to know it.
I am told that it applies to the farmer who has moved.
I would suggest that it be definitely specified in the paragraph.

I should like to follow up the remarks of the hon. member for Selkirk. In certain parts of the prairie provinces there are small towns with only one elevator each. We may have a number of towns in line, and each one may have only one elevator. Therefore, when you limit the farmer to one point of delivery you are tying him down to one elevator. If there were two or three points of delivery, then he would have the benefit of two or three elevators. If a farmer happens to live near a large town where there are six elevators he has the chance to deliver to any one of these six elevators and thereby get the
benefit of competition. But when you pin him down to deliver where there is only one elevator, even though you permit him to change that point of delivery he will still have only one elevator to which he can deliver. I have received complaints from farmers who have not been allowed to deliver to two or three points. Very often a farmer may have a large farm, and I am thinking now of the drought areas where farms often consist of two or three thousand acres. The farm may be situated halfway between two towns. Naturally that farmer wants two points of delivery. One end of the farm will be delivered at one point of delivery and the other end of the farm will be delivered at the other end. Therefore the farmer should have the right of delivery of at least two points where there are only one or two elevators at either of these points.
I am informed that where the farmer has two pieces of land, one near one delivery point and the other near another delivery point, he can have two points of delivery.

I am not talking about separate farms; I am talking about one farm situated halfway between two points. The minister is ignoring the point that the farmer is allowed only one point of delivery except where he has two farms. The point I am raising is that the farmer should be allowed to have two points of delivery where the towns are small and there is only one elevator at each point.

If a farmer comes to an
elevator and the elevator owner is in a bad mood-he may have lost a game of cribbage to the farmer the night before and has some umbrage against him-he may say to the farmer, "I am filled up, you will have to take your load back home." If he knows that the farmer has the right to go to an elevator three miles away he will not turn him down so readily. Many farmers have had to haul their grain home because they were told there was no room at the elevator, yet there was plenty of room in the elevator three miles away. I hope the minister will look into that.

Naturally, I am not
familiar with these matters in a practical way, but I am sympathetic to the questions asked. I am informed that if the purchaser names a point of delivery which is granted to him and if he is not satisfied with that and writes in to the board and asks for another point of delivery to be granted to him it will be granted.

Canadian Wheat Board Act

Why not allow him to
have both points of delivery so that he can change from one point to the other and thereby create competition?

In that case he is
running into competition with farmers who are tributary to the other elevator, and they look upon that as their delivery point.
What difference could it possibly make?

In time of congestion
it would certainly make quite a bit of difference.
There must not be any competition in a socialistic measure such as this.
The elevator may be only half-full.

On the prairies last fall
a condition arose through which some elevators were not full and at which delivery quotas could well have been raised. For some reason the board granted permission to individual growers or producers to deliver in some instances large quantities of grain. There was no general lifting of the quotas in these particular elevators, but some farmers found out about it and by simply writing or telephoning to the board they obtained permission in some instances to deliver several thousand extra bushels of grain over and above their quota, while other people did not know that it could be done.

Was it under the
regulations?

Yes. Other people did not know that it was possible even to get permission. The result was that there were some farmers who had grain on the ground because they thought they could not deliver beyond their quota. Other farmers just a few miles away got extra thousands of bushels of grain into the elevators. Since the board is taking the right to restrict deliveries in the future, what safeguard will there be to ensure equality of delivery so that other farmers in the district will know when additional bushels may be delivered to any particular elevator? Are these quotas to be lifted for one person and not for the other? Is that a general condition? If it is, is it to be changed?

I am quite satisfied
that the wheat board are ready to agree that there should be equal rights for all producers of grain so far as deliveries are concerned. Personally I have never heard of a case of

discrimination such as that mentioned by the hon. member. If discrimination such as that indicated were reported to the Canadian wheat board they would rectify it immediately.

I understand that the
wheat board gave permission for the extra deliveries.

I wish to support the remarks of the hon. member for Selkirk. I do not think that the minister clearly understands yet that there is a certain discrimination here. If I may be pardoned, I should like to offer my own case as an example. It is quite in point. I live between two towns and, while I have no bad friends in elevators at either place, the fact is that in my case the road to one town is often more suitable. This is quite unsatisfactory, owing to the fact that I have to have a special permit, and I have never seen fit to do so because ordinarily I would not haul my grain to that town. The result is that I have had to get a special permit at the end of the crop year in order to haul my grain to that specific town. Here is a case in point where, in my opinion, there is discrimination. As the hon. member for Selkirk pointed out, if there is a town in which you have a group of elevators you have a choice in the matter, but in the smaller towns there is only one elevator you are forced either to take your grain there or to change your town. It is discriminatory and should be changed for that reason.
Section 5 (section 13) agreed to.
Section 5 (section 14) agreed to.
On section 5 (section 15)-Right of producer to issue of permit book.

On page 8 in subsection 3, regarding limitation, there is this provision:
Not more than one permit book shall be issued in respect of land comprising any farm or group of farms operated as a unit.
I know of several cases where farmers have farms ten, fifteen, twenty or even fifty miles apart and it seems foolish that a man should be compelled to haul his grain a distance of fifty miles in such a case. There should be provision so that a farmer may have a permit to deliver grain to the town nearest his farm should he have two or three or half a dozen farms adjacent to other towns.

I am told that the wheat board will give permission in a case of that sort to deliver to both towns.
Section 5 (section 15) agreed to.
Section 5 (section 16) agreed to.

Canadian Wheat Board Act
On section 5 (section 17)-Powers of administration of the board.

One of the things I have been wondering about as I have read this bill is the cost to the wheat board and, therefore, to the farmer of the rather unwieldy administrative machinery which is set up. This particular section deals with permit books and so forth, and I should like to know what the actual cost of the permit books, and the machinery in connection with them, is to the wheat board, and how much extra the farmers are required to pay because of this particular system.
The cost of the quota system, permit books and so forth is paid by the government and not charged against the farmer.
What is the cost to the farmer or to the taxpayer of the country in connection with these permit books?
It is in the annual report each year.
Surely the minister can give us that figure. He must be familiar with it, or his officials must know.
I can assure my hon. friend I am not familiar with it but it can be obtained in a different place.
The minister should answer these questions.
I have answered them.

He has his officers in front of him this evening and, if he cannot get the information now, he should have it tomorrow. For him to say, "You can get it somewhere else" is not good enough, and when a proper question is asked such as this I submit that the answer should be given. The minister should not simply laugh it off.
I certainly was not trying to laugh it off.
I would ask the minister to bring that information tomorrow.
I shall be very glad to.
Thank you very much.

This is the provision of the act, in subsection 2, which the minister stated the other day he would be prepared to delete. It is a subsection under which there may be a limitation on the deliveries of grain. It provides:
The board shall, in exercising the powers conferred by this section to fix quotas for delivery of wheat by producers, fix such quotas in such manner as will ensure that the final quota for delivery from lands described in any permit 83166-56J
book in any crop year prior to or ending on the thirty-first day of July, nineteen hundred and fifty, shall be not less than 14 bushels in respect of each acre of the specified number of acres in respect of which the quota is fixed or an equivalent amount if the quota is expressed otherwise than as a quantity of wheat that may be delivered from a specified number of acres...
Yesterday the minister stated that he was prepared to delete this provision and that the government, through the board, would be ready to take delivery of all grain grown before August 1, 1950. I should like to know if the minister is prepared to take such delivery.

The minister said, when he made his statement on second reading, that he would remove subsection 2 in order to do away with any uncertainty that people might have regarding the intentions of the government. By stipulating that they would take a minimum of fourteen bushels to the acre they gave the impression that they would take only fourteen. Unfortunately, if the government strikes out subsection 2, it will make the situation worse, because under subsection 2 they guarantee that they will take a minimum of fourteen bushels. If you strike out that subsection you do not guarantee to take even fourteen. Therefore nothing would be gained by the deletion of subsection 2. The minister said, as reported at page 786 of Hansard:
Under the circumstances, with the possibility of the grain storage facilities in Canada being practically empty prior to the harvesting of the 1947 crop, the government feels that no limitation on marketings of wheat if necessary.
Merely striking out the subsection does not guarantee that the government will take delivery of all wheat produced and offered for sale prior to August 1, 1950. The mere statement that the minister made in the house does not change the wording of the act and, therefore, if he proposes to move an amendment to strike out subsection 2 of section 17, he should put something there to take its place which will give us an assurance that they will take delivery of all wheat. I think it would be better to leave subsection 2 in and add a clause stating definitely that the government is prepared to take delivery of all wheat produced and offered for sale prior to August 1, 1950. I therefore move, seconded by the member for Peace River (Mr. Low):
That subsection 2 of section 17 be amended by adding the following words:
"Notwithstanding anything contained in this act, the board shall purchase all wheat produced and offered for sale prior to July 31, 11950."
This amendment merely puts into the act what the minister has stated the government are prepared to do. If the government are
Canadian Wheat Board Act

prepared to take delivery of all wheat produced and offered for sale prior to July 31, 1950, they should have no objection to having this inserted in the act so that there may be no misunderstanding in the future.
Does the hon. member think it ought to be stated in the act that every farmer must, if the government requires, deliver all his grain before July 31, 1950?

This does not say that the farmer has to sell all his wheat before that date. That is not in the amendment at all. It says: Notwithstanding the above, the board shall purchase all wheat. They can only purchase it if the farmer offers it for sale. If the farmer does not offer it for sale, then it will not be purchased.
I understand the suggestion made is that the government should put a provision in the bill that all the wheat that is produced-
And offered for sale.
-and offered for sale in the five-year period to July 31, 1950, must be taken, but that they are not required to take anything that is not offered for sale-
No.
-and that is still on the farm. That is not going quite as far as my hon. friend went the other day.

I think we had better make this quite clear. I believe the minister knows what I have in mind. Speaking this afternoon, the Minister of Justice stated that we did not know what might happen in the later years of this agreement. We might have very large crops. The elevators might become flooded.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I did not say that.
Well, the minister said words to that effect.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I did not. Those are my hon. friend's words. That is what he stated immediately after I sat down.
The minister said we might have difficulty in taking delivery.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I did not say anything about taking delivery at all. I was talking about price entirely and the reason there would be for making prior payment.
In the event of the price falling.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Yes.

I think the minister had that in mind. The only danger there would be of the price falling would be if there was
[Mr. Quelch.l
large production and a large surplus. Then the price would fall. The two usually go together. What I had in mind was that if you had a large production of wheat and the elevators became flooded so that the government could not take delivery of all the wheat by July 31, 1950, owing to storage conditions, then that wheat might not be sold at $1.35, because there would be no guarantee that the price of $1.35 would be continued after July 31, 1950. The situation is that under this agreement the farmers are today losing anywhere from fifty to seventy-five cents a bushel; and in compensation for that the government is guaranteeing to pay $1.35 a bushel up to July 31, 1950. Therefore, in all fairness I think the minister must admit that, if the farmers are being called upon to sacrifice anywhere from fifty to seventy-five cents a bushel on all the wheat produced today and offered for sale, surely the compensating feature should apply to all wheat produced and offered for sale in the future within that pool period. Just because the elevators might become flooded should not be considered any reason why the farmers should be denied that price. The minister may ask how the government is to take delivery if the elevators are full. Provided that a system of government-approved storage were established on the farm, there would be no difficulty. The government could buy the wheat in the granaries on the farm, paying a small amount down, and the wheat could be delivered at a future day. The act already provides for paying storage.

On a point of order, might I suggest, without offering any opinion as to the pros and cons of the argument, that I do not think this is the place to discuss the matter. This section we are dealing with has to do with quotas. The other day the minister made the proposal that we would take out subsection 2 which speaks about fourteen bushels to the acre. But even if it were taken out there, it does not affect the matter of quotas. Sections 20 and 21 really deal with the matter that is now under discussion, and I think that question should be discussed there because there are some things I would want to say about it, if I were arguing the question, which I cannot say under this section.
But the minister knows very well that section 21 will be governed by section 17, by the quota.

Order. The amendment, as I have it now, reads:
Notwithstanding anything contained in this act, the board shall purchase all wheat produced and offered for sale prior to July 31, 1950.

Canadian Wheat Board Act
In my opinion this is an amendment which should be made by a minister of the crown. I think there is a suggestion that the minister give an undertaking to put the principle of this amendment into effect, but it would have to be done by a minister of the crown.
Would the minister give us that assurance now?

May I reply to the Minister of Agriculture by saying that section 21 to which he refers cannot cover the situation entirely, because section 17 governs the question of quotas; and section 21 says that the government will buy all wheat produced in the designated area, offered by a producer for sale and delivery, but it will take only what wheat the government agrees to take. If the government has a quota in effect, it will take only the amount designated in the quota. Section 17, even though you strike out subsection 2, still allows the government to set a quota.
Will the minister give the assurance that he will put the effect of the amendlment into the bill?

I do not think, as the hon. member for Acadia stated, that the striking out of this subsection is going to give to us the assurance we want with respect to the 1949 crop of wheat. What we are asking the minister now is whether the government will be prepared to take all wheat grown in 1949, even though it may not be delivered on the date of August 1, 1950, because of lack of storage space; if it was grown in 1949, will they still take it at the $1.35 initial payment or whatever the payment is for that wheat? That is the point I think we want to get cleared up.

The point of order I raised is-and although I may be wrong, it is the opinion I hold from reading the bill through-that I do not think this is the place to decide that point. That is, the question of quotas which is being decided in section 17 has to do with something which I think farmers generally are fairly well convinced we want in the act. In so far as the quota of fourteen bushels is concerned, it does not matter very much whether it is in the act or not. The difficulty our hon. friends have in Portage, for example, is that the railways are all converging on the city of Winnipeg; in numbers of places there is only one elevator; and they are concerned with the quota from one point of view. The same thing would be true near Calgary and near all the large centres.
My hon. friend may think I should have mentioned Edmonton too. They are all close

to elevators. The farmer at a distance from elevators wants the quota for this reason. He. says, "If I am living five or ten miles oul from town, I want the same opportunity to get my grain in the elevator as the fellow has who lives two miles out. I want the same space reserved for me." That is what is provided for in section 17. Over in sections 20 and 21 there are provisions made which have to do with the taking of delivery of grain which is offered for sale. I think that is where this question should be discussed. I do not think members should expect ministers or members of the committee to commit themselves, when they are discussing section 17, as to what they are going to do when we come to sections 20 and 21. I hope that we shall be able to convince members of the committee that what is being proposed by hon. members on the other side is not at all necessary in order to accomplish what is desired. If, when we come to the point of arguing it, we are not able to do that, then consideration might be given to the other suggestions that are being made. But I think it can be shown that it is not necessary to put in at any place in the act the provision which is proposed. In any event, I think this is the wrong place to discuss the matter, and it should be discussed under sections 20 and 21.

I should like to assure the minister that I am not opposing the idea of the quota. I quite realize that the quota system is absolutely necessary in western Canada, and for that reason I have no desire to see subsection 2 taken out of the act. All I want is to have the government definitely state that it will take delivery of all wheat offered for sale up to July 31, 1950.

Would the minister agree to letting this section stand. As it now reads, it is unsatisfactory. It states-
... fix such quotas in such manner as will ensure that the final quota for delivery from lands described in any permit book in any crop year prior to or ending on the 31st day of July, nineteen hundred and fifty, shall be not less than fourteen bushels . . .
And so on. I wonder if this section could be allowed to stand until we come to section 21.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
Perhaps we could come back to this in a minute or two. I should like either to move or to suggest that an amendment be made to section 17 (1) at page 8 of the bill. The amendment I would move is:
That the words "Notwithstanding any other statute or law but" be inserted between the words "may" and "subject" in the first line of section 17 (1).
Canadian Wheat Board Act

I am told that there may possibly be some conflict between some of the provisions in section 17 (1) and some provisions in the Canada Grain Act.
How would the section read as amended?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
The section as amended would read:
17. (1) The board may, notwithstanding any other statute or law, but subject to directions, if any, contained in any order of the governor in council, by order . . .
And so on. Then it would continue in its present form.	.
What difference would it make?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: It means that in any conflict between the provisions of this section and those of the Canada Grain Act, this section would prevail.

The suggested amendment gives me an opportunity to make a few observations. A few minutes ago I objected to the continuing, nature of some of the powers in this section. I refer specifically to those in section 17 (1), paragraphs (a) to (1):	I
would draw attention specifically to paragraphs (i) and (k). Paragraph (i) reads:
