(i) Require any kind of grain, or any grade or quality thereof, in any elevator to be delivered into railway cars or lake vessels.
And paragraph (k) reads:
(k) Provide for the allocation of railway cars available for the shipment of grain at any delivery point, other than ears placed pursuant to a car order book, to any elevator, loading platform or person at such delivery point.
My question is this:	Does the minister
consider, and if so why, that these extraordinary powers, which are understandable in terms of carrying out the wheat agreement, should be continued past the period of August, 1050?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Is the hon. member talking about section 17 (1) ?

Yes, and I have referred specifically to paragraphs (i) and (k) as examples. These are extraordinary powers which are understandable under the terms of carrying out the wheat agreement. But my understanding is that these powers do not cease in 1050, in the bill as it is now drafted. I foresee a strangle-hold on any potential independent trade after that period. I should like to know the purpose of it, beyond that period.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Let us examine these paragraphs one by one.

I referred to paragraphs
(i) and (k) as examples of those for which I cannot see the reason for perpetuation.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
I am informed that the
board of grain commissioners has this power now. When grain is in elevators somebody has to have power to move it forward and order it out. Therefore the section is necessary in this form to give power to require any kind of grain, or any quality thereof, to be delivered.
I can understand its present application, and I could understand it up to 1950. But am I correct in assuming that this bill perpetuates that power for eternity?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
I am informed that a
similar power is in the Canada Grain Act, and has been there for a long time; and that even after the termination of the contract it will be necessary for the wheat board to have power to order grain forward, out of the elevators.

If that
power already exists under the Canada Grain Act, why duplicate it here?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
Because the wheat board,
rather than somebody else, will be marketing it. They will be marketing all the wheat that goes into interprovincial and export trade during the currency of the contract. They may be marketing grain which they acquire after that, although this does not provide for any compulsory acquisition of grain after that.
The committee has heard the amendment read by the minister with respect to section 17 (1).

May I make a suggestion, first. Put briefly, the amendment is that, notwithstanding anything contained in any other statute, so-and-so shall prevail. I am suggesting that tills is a very broad phrase which may mean a great deal. I do not think the committee is in position at the moment to appreciate the ramifications of such a clause. Broadly speaking, I am in agreement with it because I see that they need the power. We are not going to finish this bill tonight, so that I wonder if this could not stand. No one knows better than the Minister of Justice that when you amend a bill by reference to other statutes you do not always know just where you are going without examining those other statutes. I do not think it would do any harm to let this stand. I am in favour of the principle, but I should like to know where we are going to end up when we bring in things like this, "notwithstanding any other statute".

Canadian Wheat Board Act

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I would be willing to change it to "notwithstanding anything in the Canada Grain Act," because that is the only statute that has been suggested. Would the hon. gentleman's objection still apply?
That would be much better, because I have a trifling familiarity with the Canada Grain Act. Do you not think my suggestion is a good one? We have to be careful about clauses as sweeping as that.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I will do whatever the committee wants done, but I think this is too small a point to warrant holding this up. Would it satisfy the hon. member if we changed it to "notwithstanding anything in the Canada Grain Act"?
That satisfies me.

I followed the argument a short time ago between the hon. member for Acadia and the Minister of Agriculture, but I want to be clear as to the powers conferred by subsection 2 of this section, which provides:
. . . shall be not less than fourteen bushels in respect of each acre of the specified number of acres.
I remember when the quota system was introduced in this country under which the government could receive and settle for only
280,000,000 bushels. I want to be clear that this provision is in this clause only to provide for the orderly delivery of grain, that there is not going to be a specified acreage set forth and that the board will take all the grain grown.

I understand that the minister intends to have his colleague move that this be taken out altogether. Someone on the other side said that they were not insisting on that, but I do not think it changes our intention to take out subsection 2.
Does that deprive the wheat board of the power to set quotas early in the season?
No.

I gathered that the Minister of Agriculture has the idea that by the time we got through sections 20 and 21 we would be able to see what would happen to the wheat and would be reassured that all the wheat that was produced and offered for sale would be accepted before the end of July, 1950. I wonder if it would not be wise to let section 17 stand until we have discussed sections 20 and 21? The minister will be able to make a definite statement on those
sections. Before accepting section 17, I should like to see what sections 20 and 21 will do for us.
As the hon. member for Acadia pointed out, we are greatly concerned that there shall not be a considerable amount of wheat left in the hands of the farmers at the end of July, 1950, because, if there is, it will constitute a betrayal of the farmers' interests in the light of what is going on at the present time. We want to be sure we are making provision while there is yet time.
In view of the fact that the minister has stated that it is the intention of the government to accept all the wheat grown during that period I wonder if this clause should not be-
All the grain that can be accepted for which there is space.

I think it is important that this should stand until we deal with section 21, until we understand what the govern^ ment policy is to be. We cannot be satisfied with letting the government decide by order in council whether they will accept fourteen or fifteen bushels to the acre.

May I state my contention again? It was that if we are to put in a provision such as has been suggested! by hon. members opposite, we would not put it in under section 17. If that provision were to be put in it would be put in under section 21. When we come to section 21, so far as I am concerned personally, and I think this applies to other members of the government, we will argue that it is not necessary to put that in at all, that it should not be in the bill. There are real reasons why. But nothing would be gained by letting this stand because you would not go back and put it in. It would be put in under section 21 if it were put in at all.
I have listened to this debate and I wonder whether the Minister of Trade and Commerce is in charge or whether there is a triumvirate?

The difficulty lies in the expression used by the Minister of Trade and Commerce. I gathered that he said "all the grain the government will be able to accept." That does not mean very much. I am informed that many of the annexes that were built to accommodate the grain which was being banked up, so to speak, during the war years are now being taken down in different parts of the west. I am informed that it is intended to take many more of them down. If that sort of thing goes on and we have crops of any considerable size during the next few years, will the government do
Canadian Wheat Board Act

exactly what the Minister of Trade and Commerce says they will, accept all the grain that they will be able to and then leave the farmers seriously betrayed on the whole situation? What we wish to have is some sort of definite commitment that such a thing will not occur.
For example, if we are not going to have room in the elevators or in the annexes, then some provision must be made for assistance to farmers to provide adequate storage on the farm. We shall then be sure that the farmer who produces grain will be able to sell it at $1.35 a bushel. I shall not be satisfied unless there is a definite provision in this bill to make certain that the farmers will not be betrayed.
In view of the minister's statement that the government is not going to guarantee that all the wheat grown in the year 194!) will necessarily be accepted-
I did not say that; I said that we would argue that when we reached section 21.

In view of the fact that the government will not state at this stage that all the grain grown in 1949 will be accepted; in view of the fact that the Minister of Trade and Commerce has said that it would be possible to accept all grain grown up to and including 1949; working on the basis of
22,000,000 authorized acres at fourteen bushels to the acre or 310,000,000 bushels of wheat each year the government would, according to those figures, be able to take all the crop.
There is just one fallacy in that argument. There may be 22,000,000 authorized acres, but in many years there may be many farmers who have no crop and, therefore, would have no grain to market under the fourteen bushels per authorized acre quota. My constituency is a high risk area and there may be a crop failure in 1947-I hope not-there may be one in 1948; then they may have a bumper crop in 1949 and the farmer would not be protected in any way. There is no guarantee that all the 1949 crop will be accepted when offered. In view of the minister's previous statement, I think this provision of fourteen bushels per acre for three years should be made such that a farmer could market that amount at any time he has the wheat. If, for instance, he does not have the wheat in 1947, and in 1948 has fourteen bushels per authorized acre and another fourteen bushels to take care of the authorized acreage for which he did not have a crop in 1947, over those three years he should be able to market at least an average of fourteen bushels yearly.
I do not know if I make myself clear. Provision is made for fourteen bushels per

year per acre for the three years. That is forty-two bushels per authorized acre for those years. My suggestion is that, if he does not have the wheat in 1947 or 1948 but has forty-two bushels per authorized acre even in 1949, he should be allowed to deliver that much wheat. Therefore, I move, seconded by the hon. member for Weyburn:
That subsection (2) of section 17 be amended by adding the following:
"Provided that if by reason of crop failure or other causes a producer has not in any year prior to July 34, 1950, delivered fourteen bushels in any crop year, the board shall increase the quotas for delivery by such producer in subsequent years, but not so as to increase the total quotas which a producer may deliver prior to July 31, 1950."

I am largely in sympathy with what the hon. gentleman has in mind, but I wonder if he has taken the trouble to think of a number of ways in which the amendment perhaps does not make things quite plain. The word "producer" is rather broadly defined in our act. Would the hon. member have that apply to the various persons included under that definition? Second, let us assume that a man was not a producer in the first year or the second year. Do you not think you might do better by having it apply to the land in question rather than to the person operating the land? I am broadly in sympathy with the suggestion, but I wonder if it will accomplish just what the hon. member has in mind.

I have not had time to think this through, but the suggestion might better fill the bill as I wish it to be filled. I believe the definition of a producer is broad enough. It is not only the actual producer; it would permit anyone interested in the crop, under the act, to market his share. "Producer" includes, as well as the actual producer, any person entitled as landlord, vendor or mortgagee to grain grown by an actual producer, or any share of it.

That is what bothers me. Let us say that the mortgagee has as his share two bushels per acre in a certain year. He has only two bushels of grain that year and perhaps three bushels the next year. I think if you tried it to an acreage basis, a farm basis, rather than to the individual, you probably would better accomplish what you are seeking to accomplish; and I hope the hon. member will believe that I am trying to be helpful. I can see some difficulties, however, if he just leaves the word "producer". Take a mortgagee who has only two bushels this year and three bushels next year. Perhaps he has more mortgages, and in the third year will have forty or fifty

Canadian Wheat Board Act
bushels, by spreading his interests. Surely you would not allow him, in the third year, to market that tremendous quantity of grain. He is not the original producer, so I am wondering if you would not consider tying it to the acreage rather than to the individual.

This is one indication of the trouble one gets into by proposing some of the things that are proposed. The fourteen-bushel provision was included in the first instance as a means of regulating farmers' acreage. That is what it was put in for. It was not put in on the suggestion of the government; it was put in on the suggestion of the Saskatchewan wheat pool. We had provisions under which we hoped to control acreage. It was suggested that the way to control acreage was to say we would not take more than 280,000,000 bushels of wheat, and in order to apply it to the acreage it was suggested that we should make it fourteen bushels to the acre on the established acreage, which was then 20,000,000 acres, not 22,000,000 acres as it is now; and fourteen times
20,000,000 was 280,000,000 bushels of wheat. It was thought that if we limited the quantity we would take, the acreage would be held around 22,000,000 acres. It has been in the orders in council since, and when this legislation was drafted it was transferred from the orders in council.
The position taken by the government when the matter was being argued, and when it was
first put in the orders in council, was that the provision could never be operative, for certain reasons. The only condition under which it could possibly be operative would be a condition under which the elevators could not take the grain. At the time this provision was first adopted we were emptying the elevators. We had been filling them up to 1943, but during the latter part of the war we started to empty them in order to distribute the grain that had been stored in the early years of the war. At that time we tried to point out that it would be absolutely impossible for this government or any other authority to refuse to accept grain in an elevator if the farmer had it on his farm and the elevator was not full. I think every hon. member from western Canada would agree that if we had elevators in any part of western Canada half empty and the board tried to tell the farmers they could not deliver more than fourteen bushels to the acre, and the fourteen bushels did not fill the elevators, you would not be able to keep the rest of the wheat out of those elevators. Every member of this house representing a constituency in which that was done would be writing here, sending telegrams and coming himself, trying to compel the board to open up those elevators and allow the grain to be delivered. We said that the only condition under which that could be done would be if there were a bumper crop, without sufficient markets to take care of it. The result is that it has not been necessary to apply it since it has been in here. We have been emptying the elevators. We have now got them down to where last year we had only 30,000,000 bushels of wheat left in Canada at the end of the wheat year.
A few moments ago I believe the hon. member for Lethbridge said something about storage. I thought the matter of storage would come up during the discussion, so that I obtained the figures yesterday. Prior to the war the registered elevator storage in Canada was about 423,000,000 bushels. Actually it is now 423,339,920 bushels; but in addition to that, there are 95,800,000 bushels of special storage west of the great lakes. It is perfectly right to say that most of the increased storage which was put up during the war at Fort William and from there east has been taken down, but the storage west of Fort William is 95,800,000 bushels. I do not know of any of that storage which has been taken down; practically all of that storage is still there. That makes a total of 519,000,000 bushels. I think we can say that there is no possibility in the world of our meeting in 1947 a condition where we shall require 519,000,000 bushels of storage space in order to handle the wheat
Canadian Wheat Board Act

which will be available in Canada to fill storage space at any particular time during that year.
Every country in the world which imports wheat will be begging us for wheat, and we shall be pressing our railways all across Canada all through 1947 to get that wheat to the ports just as fast as they can get it here. So far as I am concerned, I think that will be the condition if not all through 1948, at least well into that year. With a situation of that kind which I do not think anyone can question, it is a mistake to have in this bill-I thought it was a mistake as soon as I saw it there and I still think it is a mistake-anything about fourteen bushels to the acre being delivered to elevators or to give anyone authority to say anything about fourteen bushels to the acre. What we ought to be doing, in the next two years anyway and maybe for much longer, is pushing grain through these elevators as fast as we can push it through, getting it in and out again, getting it on down to the ports. At times we may even have to refuse the suggestion that there will be any quota on it at all in order to get space for the men who are ten miles or fifteen miles back. We may find that it is not necessary for the board to say that there will be any quota at all during the seasons which are immediately ahead of us. We may want the men who are within two miles, three miles or four miles to shove their grain in and get it shipped to get boats loaded. It all depends on shipping facilities and other things which may develop as we go along. With that situation in front of us, I do not think the government should be bound, nor should the wheat board be bound, to do any of these particular things that are talked about at the moment.
It may be taken for granted that the government, the wheat board and everyone associated with it will be getting this grain through just as fast as we can get it through.
With regard to the suggestion that we should put a provision in the bill that anyone who, because of drought or for any other reason, is not able to deliver grain to the elevator to the amount of fourteen bushels to the acre for one or two or three years should be permitted to deliver forty-two bushels to the acre, I cannot conceive of anything that might run you into more trouble. There are certain people who will refuse to believe, whether hon. members on this side of the house or hon. members of the C.C.F. party believe it or not, that this thing is going to last for four years. Knowing western farmers as I do, if they get the idea that wheat is going to be higher later on, they will hold back their wheat, and they'

may hold back much more than forty bushels to the acre for every acre on which they are growing wheat. For anyone to say that, after a man has done that, the wheat board or the government must give absolute commitment that they will take all that grain and by doing so maybe leave some other fellow who has done what we have been trying to get him to do, namely deliver his grain every year, put it in the elevators and let it get to the people who require it for food, he will be asking us to say to him, you have to take your chance; sit back and let the other fellow get his forty-two bushels in. These are possibilities that we have to look at; if we are to look at all the possibilities along the way and try to cover it all by this legislation, I do not think it will be possible to get legislation that will be suitable at all.
When hon. members who read this bill for the first time said the other day that the fourteen bushels to the acre ought to come out, I think they were right. I think we should still take the position that the fourteen bushels ought to come out. The wheat board and, the government ought to be left in the position to handle the quotas as they go along in a manner -which will best suit the producer himself, because we want to suit the producer. We want to do for him that which he feels ought to be done, just as every hon. member does. But the thing that will best suit the producer must at the same time make it possible to have the grain moved as rapidly as possible to where it is wanted. Therefore I say the less that we put in the act in the way of commitments of that kind, the better. Everyone is going to be working for the same end, anyway. We must have a certain amount of faith and confidence in one another, and that is not asking very much. When we come to section 21 I think that will be the time to discuss the question that is in the minds of hon. members and, until we have either convinced them or at least convinced a sufficient number to have the legislation put through in its present form, we should continue along that line. If we cannot do that, then we may have to submit to something else.
I think this section would be a much better section if we took subsection 2 out of it as was proposed, and leave the section as it would be without subsection 2. We can consider the other question when we come to it.

In view of the argument we have just listened to, probably the hon. member will be ready to withdraw his motion. I have been very happy in listening to the discourse in the past few minutes. I

Canadian Wheat Board Act
am glad that the Minister of Agriculture has had a change of heart. I could not help but notice the expression on the face of the Minister of Mines and Resources, because I thought of the speeches delivered by the two ministers and reports that I had read which had been delivered on the prairies within the last few months, pointing out how the farmers of the prairies would appreciate this wheat agreement with Britain, because there would be no demand for wheat in the latter part of 1947 and certainly not at all in 1948. Because of that, the farmers would be happy to have this wheat contract. I am glad the Minister of Agriculture has become a convert, and we are now to have a demand for wheat for the length of time that he has told us, which will solve a lot of our problems. Because of that, I am sure the amendment will not be taken as seriously as it otherwise would.

Since I was the mover of the amendment, with the permission of the seconder I shall be glad to withdraw it, if the minister is going to have the clause deleted. However, I wish to refute one argument which the minister raised. He said that quite a few of the farmers are going to hold back their grain. I wish to remind him that in the southwest part of the province there have been two crop failures. Quite a large number of people are living off family allowances and selling the odd cow.
There have been three of them.

These people are not going to hold back their grain. What I had hoped to do was to make it possible for these people who could not deliver fourteen bushels in one year but who may have a crop in three years, to market their grain.

After listening to the Minister of Agriculture tonight, I am more convinced that this section should stand until we have had a chance to discuss section 21. When the hon. member for Acadia spoke the other night he tried to put across the idea that the wheat growers are not going to be satisfied with the guarantee of fourteen bushels for the twenty-two million acres of wheat for each year during the contract. I understood from the Minister of Agriculture that night that it was the intention of the government to accept all the wheat that would be produced on those twenty-two million acres during the period, but I notice from the speech of the Minister of Trade and Commerce that he carefully protected the government by commitments with respect to wheat for which storage was provided. I submit that, if we
want to maintain production over an extended period, we must be prepared to give guarantees to people for specific amounts. The hon. member for Melfort happens to live in a good wheat producing area, and on his own farm for twenty-five years he has produced an average of thirty bushels for every seeded acre. Are the farmers in that area to be satisfied with removing the fourteen-bushel clause, leaving it to the government to determine by order in council the number of bushels that will be accepted on the authorized acreage?
I think that cabinet ministers who are piloting the bill through should agree to allow the section to stand until we come to section 21 and find out what the government is prepared to suggest.

I submit, Mr. Chairman, you are not in order in putting the amendment to a vote while a member is on his feet. I feel I must appeal from your ruling, if that is your ruling. I submit that you cannot put the motion while a member is on his feet.

I asked all members who were in favour of 'the amendment moved by the Minister of Justice to indicate accordingly. I did not make a ruling, but hon. members said "carried."

I was on my feet, Mr. Chairman. I thought you were rising to discuss a question of order and I sat down. I thank you for permitting me to continue. Several hon. members, I believe, have argued at considerable length that the wheat producer should have some guarantee as to how many bushels will be accepted during the period. There is some suggestion that a guarantee of

fourteen bushels is not sufficient. If we pass this section and leave it to the government to determine by order in council the number of bushels, we place the wheat producers in the position where they will have no idea how many bushels they can deliver for the period of the contract. I urge that hon. members support me in voting down the minister's motion to delete subsection 2 of section 17. I think it should stand until section 21 has been discussed.
The Minister of Justice moved an amendment and I asked those in favour of the amendment so to state. I understood that the amendment was carried.
Oh, no.
Then I will ask the members again.

The hon. member was on his feet when you stood up to put the motion, Mr. Chairman. At the present time, under subsection 2 of section 17, we have a guarantee that the government will take up to fourteen bushels, but if you strike out subsection 2 we have no guarantee that they will take even fourteen bushels. I suggest, as other hon. members have suggested, that we wait until we reach section 21 and find out the intentions of the government before striking out this provision. We should allow subsection 2 of section 17 to stand until we know the intentions of the government. The Minister of Agriculture, speaking a few minutes ago, said he was satisfied that there would be plenty of room for all wheat we could deliver up to the end of the period. If that is so, the government should not hestitate to give a guarantee that they will accept delivery of all wheat that can be produced and offered for sale in that period. The Minister of Agriculture would not make that statement if he were not satisfied on the point. I have no doubt he may be right and, if the Minister of Agriculture is right, then the government should not hesitate to give that guarantee. But it is not satisfactory simply to have it by word of mouth. Who knows whether this government will be in power in 1950? There may be another government in power.
A worse one.

And that government will be bound only by whatever is in the act. We want that guarantee put in the act now. Personally, I am not prepared to have subsection 2 removed, because it does give a guarantee of fourteen bushels. Certainly before that 
guarantee of fourteen bushels is removed I want to have some other provision put in to take its place.

If I may deal with this question further I thought-and I am sure I am speaking within the memory of other members of the house-that the members who are speaking now were very insistent the other night that they would not allow the bill to go past the second reading until we agreed to take the fourteen bushels out.
The minister was asked for a guarantee to take delivery of all wheat produced and offered for sale prior to July 31, 1950.

I am not saying that the hon. member who has spoken did, but the other hon. members were insistent in regard to the fourteen bushels. The minister came down the next day and read a statement to the house in which he said he was agreeable to do that, and the house applauded.
On your side.
No, on the other side.
Not here.
This side did not say anything about it. I felt like applauding myself but as a matter of fact I did not.
It is hard) to hear the minister sometimes.

The hon. member must be hard of hearing. I do not know that we should insist on this section going through tonight if everyone is so insistent on its remaining open until another day. If we talk for another ten minutes it will not go through anyway. However I would suggest to hon. members that there is something in the suggestion that they might find a little difficult.
I do not think any piece of legislation can be one-sided, and when you say that the government must do a certain thing, there are some people who must see to it as well that the funds which the government is handling are protected, because they are not the government's funds but the funds of the people. If we try to visualize what conditions will be four years from now, I can think of conditions under which we might need far more power than we have now in order to get delivery of wheat. This bill does not say that we can go to anyone's farm and take his wheat and put it on the'market. All it says is that if a farmer delivers wheat to an elevator we must buy it and the wheat board must take delivery of the wheat.

If there is room.

Canadian Wheat Board Act

Yes, if it is delivered there and there is room, they must take it. It says that. But assuming that we do get down in the end, as some people have been predicting ever since this agreement was made, to a condition where the price is going down, there is not any difficulty about what will happen. Every farmer in the country will be trying to get his wheat into the elevator and have it sold at $1.35 a bushel before a lower initial payment is made on it. But I can conceive of an entirely different condition developing where, if we continue the pool beyond 1950, we may have to set a higher initial payment, say $1.45. Immediately that is realized, we shall not be able to get any wheat from the farmers and into the elevators.
I think, if we must put into that bill a provision which says we shall take all the wheat which is delivered at the elevator at a time when we do not know what the conditions are going to be, we must also put into the bill a provision, that if any wheat grown before that date is delivered at any time after that date, we cannot pay any higher price for it than $1.35 a bushel. You can get into all kinds of difficulties by simply trying to imagine what the condition will be at the end of this contract. But section 20 of this contract says that when you begin to decide what is going to happen after 1950, this bill must be brought into the house, not after 1950 but before then, and conditions must be discussed as they then are. When this bill is brought into the house for amendment, the government no longer has control over it; it is in the hands of this house and they can do anything they like about it at that time, having all the facts in front of them. I think that is a much more reasonable position in which to leave the legislation than to try to guess what the condition will be four years from now. Provision is made in the bill for the protection of everyone, if legislation brought before this house ever protects anyone. Provision is made for giving every farmer in western Canada the protection afforded by the opportunity for the House of Commons to say what is to happen. That being the case, I think we are trying to do something which is absolutely impossible for anyone to do, namely to surmise or predict what will happen or what we ought to do in order to protect ourselves against what may happen. If we start trying to protect the farmer in one direction, we shall have to try to protect the taxpayer in the other, and this legislation might be a peculiar looking document by the time we got through with it and not meet the requirements at all. I would suggest, if the minister would concur,
that we let the whole thing stand from there on until another day, think it over and come back and discuss it then.

Just before that is done, I wish to ask the minister a simple question on the simple reply that he gave to the question a moment ago. The speech he has just made is based on the proposition that no one can surmise what will happen. Is not his whole contract with Great Britain built on surmise for the years 1945 to 1950, and that surmise made by the government itself? Do not worry the rest of us about surmising. The government started it.

Before this bill is allowed to stand, I should like to ask a question based on the remarks made by the Minister of Agriculture a while ago with regard to transportation. The idea has grown up across the country that our transportation of grain is held up owing to bad weather and so on, but it goes back quite a bit farther than that. I should like to know what control the wheat board has or how it has handled the matter of obtaining the necessary cars for the shipment of grain. I wish to quote the first part of a paragraph from the Current Review of "Agricultural Conditions in Canada", of December, 1946. It is there stated.
It is estimated that Canada's export of wheat and wheat flour equivalent during the first four months of the 1946-47 season totalled approximately 75 million bushels as compared with 154 million for the corresponding period a year ago. This situation is largely due to the fact that Canada's export programme was thrown off schedule early in the crop year. At the beginning of the season, lakehead stocks were at a very low level and only minimum supplies were available in export positions.
Then further down on the same page:
Up to November 28 more than 216 million bushels of wheat had been delivered at country points. Deliveries to the same date last year amounted to 156 million bushels. With the seasonal decline in marketings under way, a much lower rate of delivery is expected to prevail over the remainder of the crop year.
That also has a far-reaching effect, as you know, because of the cost of transportation. The long rail haul from the lakehead to the eastern part of the country is much more expensive. That is an added expense which will have to be borne by the board and will be, I should think, an added expense to the producer in the handling of this grain.
No.
